m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Check that your computer, browser, and webcam are ready for Teachable Machine.
  • Allow camera (and microphone) access in the browser and in your operating system.
  • Explain where your samples are stored, and what leaves your computer only when you choose.
  • Pick the webcam path or the photo-upload path for the course.

By the end of this course you will have trained a computer to tell rock from paper from scissors, to sort recycling from trash, and to drive a small game with your hands. You won't write a line of code, install anything, or make an account to do it. All of it happens on one web page: Teachable Machine, a free tool from Google at teachablemachine.withgoogle.com.

Teachable Machine trains real machine learning models. The model it builds for your hand signs is the same kind of image classifier that sorts photos on a phone, just smaller. That also means it makes real mistakes, and much of this course is about spotting those mistakes and fixing the data that caused them.

#What you need

Item Needed? Notes
A laptop, desktop, or Chromebook Yes The page puts three panels side by side, so a full-size screen is much easier than a phone.
A current web browser Yes Chrome is the safest choice. Details below.
An internet connection Yes, to load the page Training itself runs on your computer, not on a server.
A webcam Recommended The built-in camera on a laptop or Chromebook is fine.
A microphone Only for sound projects Built-in is fine.
A Google account No Only needed if you want to save projects to Google Drive.

No webcam? You can still do every project. Teachable Machine also accepts photos you upload, so you can take pictures with a phone, move them to the computer, and drag them in. The lessons point out where the upload path differs.

#Which browser to use

Teachable Machine runs inside the browser, and some browsers handle the camera and microphone better than others. When something goes wrong with recording, the site itself suggests Chrome or Firefox.

Windows

Use Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge. Edge is built on the same engine as Chrome, so it behaves the same way here. Firefox also works.

Check that your browser is up to date: in Chrome, open the ⋮ menu, then Help › About Google Chrome. It updates itself if it's behind.

macOS

Use Google Chrome or Firefox. Safari loads the site, but sound projects can misbehave in it: you may see "Your browser does not support recording playable audio; however you can still create a model." Image and pose projects are less affected, but switching to Chrome saves trouble.

Chromebook

Use the built-in Chrome browser. Nothing to install.

On a school-managed Chromebook, your administrator controls camera access and can block some sites. If the camera never turns on in Teachable Machine but works in the Camera app, the block is probably a school setting, and the photo-upload path will still work.

#Let the browser use your camera

The first time you click Webcam in a project, the browser asks whether the site may use your camera. In Chrome the choices are Allow while visiting the site, Allow this time, and Never allow. Choose one of the first two.

If you click Never allow by accident, the camera stays dark and Teachable Machine shows "There was an error opening your webcam. Make sure permissions are enabled or switch to image uploading." To undo it, click the site-information icon at the left end of the address bar, switch Camera on, and reload the page.

Your operating system has its own permission switch underneath the browser's, and both have to be on:

Windows

Windows 11: open Start › Settings › Privacy & security › Camera. Turn on Camera access, and further down turn on Let desktop apps access your camera. Browsers count as desktop apps.

Windows 10: open Start › Settings › Privacy › Camera, check that camera access for this device is on, and switch on Allow desktop apps to access your camera.

If a video-call app such as Teams or Zoom has the camera open, close it first; Windows often lets only one app use the camera at a time.

macOS

Open the Apple menu › System Settings › Privacy & Security › Camera and turn the switch on for your browser. The browser only appears in that list after it has asked for the camera once, so open Teachable Machine and click Webcam first. If the camera still doesn't start after you flip the switch, quit the browser completely and reopen it.

Chromebook

Open Settings and search for camera. Make sure camera access is on for the Chromebook, then check the site permission in Chrome as described above. Some Chromebooks also have a physical privacy switch or shutter beside the camera, so check that it's open.

For sound projects the steps are the same with Microphone in place of Camera.

#Where your samples go

This is the most important page of setup, because you'll be recording faces, hands, voices, and rooms. Teachable Machine's own FAQ is clear about it: your samples are not sent to any servers, and training happens inside your browser tab. The photos you record live in that tab's memory, on your computer.

Something leaves your computer only when you choose one of these actions:

  • Save project to Drive copies your samples into your own Google Drive. They are yours, and only people you share the file with can see them.
  • Download project as file saves everything to a file on your computer. Nothing goes online.
  • Upload my model (in the export screen, covered later) publishes the trained model so you can use it in a website. The model goes to Google's servers; the photos and recordings you trained it with do not. Anyone who has the link can use the model.
  • Closing the tab without saving throws everything away. Nothing stays in the browser or on a server.

So the default is private, and every step that shares something is one you take on purpose. Keep that in mind when other people appear in your samples. Module 1's third lesson sets the consent rules this course follows.

#Choose your path

You'll pick one of two ways to collect examples. You can switch at any time.

Webcam path Upload path
How you add samples Hold a button and record frames live Take photos elsewhere and drag them in
Speed Fast: dozens of samples in seconds Slower: you take each photo
Best for Hand signs, poses, objects you can hold up No webcam, a blocked camera, or a dataset you want to reuse
Testing the model Live, in front of the camera Upload new photos into the preview

Most learners use the webcam path and fall back to uploads for testing, because uploading photos taken in a different room is an easy way to test a model on places it has never seen.

⚠️ Watch out

The classic setup trap: the camera works in one app but not in the browser. That almost always means one of the two permission layers is off, or another app is holding the camera. Close video-call apps, check the operating system switch, check the browser's site permission, then reload the page. Reloading matters: the page asks for the camera when it opens it, not continuously.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You record 200 photos of your hands, train a model, and close the tab without saving. Where are the photos now?

  • Nothing goes to Drive unless you choose Save project to Drive and log in.

  • The FAQ says samples are not sent to any servers; training happens in your tab.

  • The samples lived in the tab's memory. Closing it without saving deletes them, which is why the next lessons show you how to save.

Show answer

C. The samples lived in the tab's memory. Closing it without saving deletes them, which is why the next lessons show you how to save.

2The browser says the camera is allowed, but Teachable Machine still shows an error opening your webcam. What should you check next?

  • The browser's permission sits on top of the system's. Both must allow it, and only one app may be able to use the camera at a time.

  • No account is needed for the camera or for training.

  • Both image models use the webcam the same way.

Show answer

A. The browser's permission sits on top of the system's. Both must allow it, and only one app may be able to use the camera at a time.

3You click Upload my model to use your model on a website. What does Google receive?

  • The FAQ says the training examples are not published with the model.

  • The model is a file of learned numbers. Your photos stay on your computer unless you save them to Drive.

  • Uploading publishes the model so a link can load it.

Show answer

B. The model is a file of learned numbers. Your photos stay on your computer unless you save them to Drive.

Key takeaways

  • Teachable Machine needs only a current browser on a laptop, desktop, or Chromebook; a webcam is recommended and uploads work without one.
  • Camera access has two layers, the browser's site permission and the operating system's switch, and both must be on.
  • Samples stay in your browser tab and training runs there too. Saving to Drive, downloading, and uploading a model are the only ways anything leaves, and each is your choice.
  • Closing the tab without saving deletes your work.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): the official answers on privacy, saving, and exporting. The "Saving & Exporting" section is the one to read now.
  • Use your camera and microphone in Chrome (opens in a new tab): Google's help page for site permissions and choosing which camera Chrome uses.
  • Manage app permissions for your camera in Windows (opens in a new tab): Microsoft's step-by-step guide, with pictures, for Windows 10 and 11.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start a Standard image model project from the Teachable Machine home page.
  • Find the three panels: classes on the left, Training in the middle, Preview on the right.
  • Rename classes, record samples with Hold to Record, and train a model.
  • Prove the model works by watching its preview bars change.

The fastest way to understand Teachable Machine is to use it once from start to finish before learning why any of it works. You'll build the smallest useful model there is: one that answers a single question, is there a thumbs-up in the picture or not? It takes about five minutes, and the last minute is the fun one.

Here is the whole loop you're about to run. Every project in the course follows it.

#Step 1: Open an image project

  1. Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com and click Get Started.
  2. The New Project page shows three cards: Image Project, Audio Project, and Pose Project. Below them are links to open an existing project from Google Drive or from a file, which you'll use in the next lesson.
  3. Click Image Project. A box asks which kind of image model you want.
  4. Choose Standard image model ("Best for most uses"). It works on 224 × 224 pixel color images.

The other choice, Embedded image model, makes a much smaller model from 96 × 96 grayscale images, meant for tiny microcontroller boards. You won't need it in this course.

#Step 2: Find your way around the screen

The project opens with three columns:

  • Left: your classes. Two cards called Class 1 and Class 2, each with Add Image Samples: and two buttons, Webcam and Upload. Below them is Add a class.
  • Middle: Training. A Train Model button, and under it an Advanced section that you'll open in Module 3.
  • Right: Preview. An Export Model button and a message: "You must train a model on the left before you can preview it here."

A class is one of the answers the model is allowed to give. This model gets two: thumbs up, and nothing.

#Step 3: Name the classes

Click the pencil icon next to Class 1 and type Thumbs up. Then rename Class 2 to Nothing.

Names don't change how the model learns, but they're what the preview shows, and a model with labels like "Class 1" is confusing a month later. Two classes can't share the same name; Teachable Machine refuses to train if they do.

#Step 4: Record the thumbs-up class

  1. On the Thumbs up card, click Webcam. Allow the camera if the browser asks. A live square view of your camera appears.
  2. Hold your thumb up in view. Press and hold the Hold to Record button. While you hold it, Teachable Machine grabs frames from the camera many times a second (the default setting is 24).
  3. While recording, move a little: tilt your hand, bring it closer, pull it back, switch hands. Release after four or five seconds.

The card now says something like 87 Image Samples, with a row of thumbnails. Click any thumbnail to see it larger; from there you can delete it or move it to another class.

💡 Tip

Sitting still while you record gives you 80 nearly identical photos, which teach the model about as much as 5 would. Small movements give it variety for free. Module 2 is all about this.

#Step 5: Record the "nothing" class

On the Nothing card, click Webcam and record about the same number of samples with no thumbs-up: your face, your hand resting flat, an empty chair, your hand waving. Aim for a count within about 10 of the first class.

Why bother with a "nothing" class? Because a model can only answer with the classes you gave it. With only a Thumbs up class, every picture would be a thumbs-up, including an empty room. The Nothing class gives it somewhere else to put its answer.

#Step 6: Train

Click Train Model. The button changes to Preparing training data..., then Training..., and a moment later to Model Trained. On most laptops this takes well under a minute for a couple of hundred images.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't switch tabs while it trains. Teachable Machine shows "Don't switch tabs! You must leave this tab open to train your model." Browsers slow down tabs you aren't looking at, so leaving can pause training or make it crawl. Stay on the page until the button reads Model Trained.

#Step 7: Test it in the preview

The Preview panel wakes up as soon as training finishes. Input is switched ON, the webcam is selected, and under Output there's a bar for each class with a percentage.

Now try it. Hold up a thumbs-up, then put your hand down, then hold it up again. Here's what success looks like:

The two percentages always add up to 100%, because the model is splitting its answer between your two classes. Module 4 explains what those numbers do and don't mean.

🧪 Try it yourself

Make a thumbs-down. The model has never seen one, so it has to choose between the two answers it knows. Which bar wins, and by how much? Then try a fist, and a peace sign. Write down what happens; you'll explain it in Module 2.

#No webcam? The upload path

On each class card, click Upload instead of Webcam. You'll see "Choose images from your files, or drag & drop here". Drag in .png or .jpg photos; Teachable Machine crops each to a square. Twenty or more photos per class is enough for this test.

To test, switch the preview's input from Webcam to File using the menu beside the Input toggle, and upload a photo the model hasn't seen.

#When it doesn't work

  • "There was an error opening your webcam." Permission is blocked, or another app has the camera. Go back to the permission steps in the previous lesson, then reload.
  • Train Model is grayed out or shows an error. Every class that is switched on needs at least one sample, and an empty card blocks training. Check both cards for a sample count.
  • Training seems frozen. You probably switched tabs. Return to the tab and wait, or click Train Model again.
  • The preview is stuck on one class no matter what you do. Usually the two classes look too similar, or one has far more samples than the other. Record more varied samples for the weaker class and train again.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You train a model with a Thumbs up class and a Nothing class, then show it a thumbs-down. What will the bars show?

  • The model never abstains. It always splits 100% across the classes you gave it.

  • It has to pick from what it knows. A thumbs-down shares a lot with a thumbs-up (a fist, one finger out), so the result can go either way.

  • Teachable Machine only shows the classes you created.

Show answer

B. It has to pick from what it knows. A thumbs-down shares a lot with a thumbs-up (a fist, one finger out), so the result can go either way.

2Why record the thumbs-up while moving your hand, instead of holding perfectly still?

  • Identical frames add almost no information. Different angles and distances help it recognize the gesture anywhere in the frame.

  • Training time depends on how many samples you have, not how varied they are.

  • It keeps every frame you record.

Show answer

A. Identical frames add almost no information. Different angles and distances help it recognize the gesture anywhere in the frame.

Key takeaways

  • Get Started › Image Project › Standard image model opens a project with classes on the left, Training in the middle, and Preview on the right.
  • Hold to Record captures frames while you hold the button; moving while you record gives you variety.
  • A model can only answer with the classes you made, so a "nothing" class matters.
  • Stay on the tab while it trains, then test live in Preview.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine (opens in a new tab): the home page has three short official tutorials (a banana ripeness meter, a snap-clap-whistle sound model, and a head-tilt pose model) worth trying after this lesson.
  • Teachable Machine community repository (opens in a new tab): the code behind the tool and the export snippets. You don't need it yet, but it shows what's happening under the buttons.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save a Teachable Machine project to a file or to Google Drive, and open it again later.
  • Keep a short project log of classes, sample counts, and who appears in the data.
  • Follow the consent rules for recording yourself and other people.
  • Record without holding the mouse button, and fix the five most common problems.

Teachable Machine has no autosave. If you record 300 samples, train a great model, and then your laptop restarts for an update, all of it is gone. The FAQ puts it plainly: if you close the tab without saving, nothing is saved in your browser or on any servers. If you try to leave a project with unsaved changes, the page asks you to confirm, but that only helps if you're there to see it.

So the first habit of this course is saving, and the second is knowing whose face is in your data.

#Four ways to keep your work

Open the menu with the ☰ icon at the top left of a project (next to the Teachable Machine name). The saving options live there, and the FAQ lists four ways to keep work:

Option Where to find it What it keeps Where it goes
Download project as file ☰ menu Classes, samples, and training settings A .tm file on your computer
Save project to Drive ☰ menu The same, as a file Your own Google Drive
Download Samples ⋮ menu on one class card That class's samples A zip file on your computer
Export Model Preview panel The trained model only, no samples A download or a link (Module 6)

For this course, Download project as file is the one to use every time. It needs no account, works on school computers, and keeps everything private. Do it at the end of every session, and before any experiment that might wreck a model you like.

#Save to a file and open it again

  1. In your project, open ☰ and choose Download project as file.
  2. The browser saves a file ending in .tm to your Downloads folder. Rename it right away (see the naming pattern below).
  3. To reopen it later, go to the home page, click Get Started, and choose Open an existing project from a file. Or, inside any project, open ☰ › Open project from file.
  4. Pick your .tm file. Your classes and samples come back, but the model doesn't: click Train Model again. With the same samples that takes a few seconds.

Opening a project replaces whatever is on screen, so save the current one first.

#Save to Google Drive (optional)

☰ › Save project to Drive asks you to Log in to Google Drive, then to name the project. Later, Open project from Drive brings it back, and you can share the Drive file with a teammate so they can keep working on it.

Two cautions. Many school Google accounts block third-party apps from Drive, so this may fail on a school login even though it works at home. And a Drive file can be shared by accident; if your samples include other people, keep them in a file on your own computer instead.

#Name and organize your files

Make one folder for the course, such as c4t-ml-models, and give every saved project a name that says what it is, which version it is, and when you made it:

Keep old versions instead of overwriting them. In Module 3 you'll compare a lopsided dataset with a balanced one, and you can only compare what you kept.

#Keep a project log

Machine learning projects go wrong in ways you can only diagnose if you remember what you did. Keep a plain text file (or a page in a notebook) with one entry per version:

The People line is the one most projects skip, and the one that matters most.

#The consent rules for this course

The samples you record are personal data: faces, hands, voices, bedrooms. Treat them that way.

  1. Record only people who said yes, after you told them what you're recording, what for, and where it will be kept. A shrug is not a yes. For anyone under 18, sharing their images beyond your own computer also needs a parent or guardian's okay.
  2. Check the background before you hold the button. Family members walking past, photos on the wall, a screen showing messages, and mail with an address all end up in your samples.
  3. Don't use other people's photos from the internet for classes about people. Objects (cans, bottles, fruit) are fine.
  4. Delete what you don't need. If someone changes their mind, remove their samples with the class's ⋮ menu or the thumbnail viewer, retrain, and save a new version.
  5. Share models, not datasets. An exported model doesn't contain your photos, which makes it much safer to share than the .tm file.

#Record without holding the button

Hold to Record asks you to keep a mouse button pressed while also posing for the camera. That's awkward with one hand, and impossible for some people. There's a setting for it:

  1. Click Webcam on a class card, then the Settings button on the webcam view.
  2. Switch Hold to Record to OFF.
  3. Set Delay (seconds before recording starts; the default is 2) and Duration (how long it records; the default is 6). Leave FPS at 24.
  4. Click Save Settings. Now one click starts a countdown, then records for the set time on its own.

This is also the best way to record yourself at a distance, such as full-body poses: click, step back, and pose.

#Fixes for the problems that stop beginners

What you see Likely cause Fix
"There was an error opening your webcam." Permission blocked, or another app has the camera Close video-call apps, allow the camera in the browser and the OS, reload
"Could not open your camera. You may have denied access." You clicked Never allow Site-information icon in the address bar › turn Camera on › reload
Training stops or crawls You switched tabs Stay on the tab until the button reads Model Trained
"More than one class with label … was found." Two classes share a name Rename one; every label must be unique
The project you opened has no model Project files keep samples, not a trained model Click Train Model
Everything vanished Tab closed or browser restarted without saving Nothing to recover; save to a file every session from now on

📝 Note

Your microphone has the same two permission layers as your camera. If a sound project says "There was an error opening your microphone," use the same fixes with Microphone in place of Camera.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You reopen yesterday's .tm file and the Preview panel says you must train a model first. What went wrong?

  • A damaged file wouldn't open at all.

  • Click Train Model. With the same samples you'll get a very similar model in seconds.

  • Drive saves the same project contents as the file does.

Show answer

B. Click Train Model. With the same samples you'll get a very similar model in seconds.

2Your friend agreed to appear in your gesture dataset last month but now wants out. What's the right sequence?

  • Their face is still in the data. Agreement can be taken back, and the samples must go.

  • Removing the samples and retraining means the new model was never trained on them, and saving a new version keeps your log accurate.

  • The current model was still trained on their images. Retrain without them first.

Show answer

B. Removing the samples and retraining means the new model was never trained on them, and saving a new version keeps your log accurate.

Key takeaways

  • Nothing saves automatically. Use ☰ › Download project as file at the end of every session, and rename the .tm file with a name, version, and date.
  • Reopening a project restores samples and settings; you retrain to get the model back.
  • Record only people who agreed, check the background, and share models rather than datasets.
  • Turn Hold to Record off in webcam Settings to record with a countdown instead of holding the button.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ: Saving & Exporting (opens in a new tab): what each save option keeps and who can see a published model.
  • People + AI Guidebook: Data Collection + Evaluation (opens in a new tab): Google's guide for designers on collecting data responsibly, including consent and who is represented.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what a class is and why the model must always pick one of them.
  • Test a set of classes for overlap and for differences a single frame can't show.
  • Plan how many examples each class needs, and why similar counts matter.
  • Vary lighting, angle, distance, background, and people across every class.
  • Keep people who didn't agree out of your data.

Priya builds a gesture controller for a racing game with four classes: Left (pointing left), Right (pointing right), Boost (waving), and Stop (open palm). In her room it works. At a friend's house it calls everything Boost, and pointing left is Stop half the time. Then she scrolls through her samples and finds her little brother in the background of forty of them. He never agreed to be in it.

None of these are training problems. Training did exactly what it was told. They're data problems, decided before she pressed Train Model: which classes she chose, and which examples she gave each one.

#A class is an answer the model has to choose

A class is one of the labels the model is allowed to output. The model's whole job is: given one input, decide which of your classes it belongs to. It cannot say "none of these," and it cannot say "two of these." Every input gets split across your classes, with the shares adding up to 100%.

That one fact gives you two rules:

  1. Classes must not overlap. Each possible input should belong to exactly one class. "Open palm" and "Hand" overlap, because an open palm is a hand. When classes overlap, the model is trained to give two different answers to the same picture, and its scores land somewhere in the middle.
  2. You need a class for "none of the above." If people will sometimes show the camera nothing useful, make a Nothing (or Background) class with examples of exactly that. Otherwise an empty chair gets labeled as whichever class it happens to resemble.

#Can one frame show the difference?

A Teachable Machine image model looks at one frame at a time. It has no idea what happened a moment ago. That's why Priya's Boost class failed: waving is a motion, and a single frame of a wave is just an open hand at an angle. It looks like Stop.

Before you commit to a set of classes, run this test on each pair: if I showed a friend one still photo, could they name the class in a second?

Weak class set Problem Stronger version
Wave, Still hand Needs motion; one frame can't show it Open palm, Fist
Hand, Thumbs up Overlap: a thumbs-up is a hand Thumbs up, Flat hand, Nothing
Happy, Excited People can't agree on the boundary Smiling, Not smiling
Plastic, Bottle Overlap: many bottles are plastic Recycling, Trash, Nothing

#How many examples each class needs

Teachable Machine doesn't start from zero. The FAQ explains that image and pose models are built on a pretrained network called MobileNet, and your classes become only its last step. MobileNet already learned edges, textures, and shapes from more than a million labeled photos, so it needs your examples only to learn how your classes differ. That's why tens of examples can work instead of tens of thousands.

Some numbers to plan with:

  • Images: Teachable Machine will train with as little as one sample per class, but plan on 50 to 150 per class for a model you'd trust in front of other people.
  • Sounds: Audio projects insist on at least 8 samples per class and at least 20 seconds of background noise. Each sample is a one-second clip.
  • Similar counts in every class. If one class has 300 examples and another has 30, the model leans toward the big one. Module 3 shows exactly why.

There's a hidden reason to avoid tiny classes. When you train, Teachable Machine quietly sets aside 15% of each class's samples as test samples it never trains on, to check itself. With 20 samples in a class, only 3 are held back, and a check based on 3 photos tells you very little.

#Variety: vary what shouldn't matter, in every class

A model learns whatever is different between your classes. It doesn't know which difference you meant. If every Rock sample was taken with the lamp on and every Paper sample after sunset, then brightness is a perfectly good way to tell the classes apart, and the model may learn that instead of hands. It looks brilliant in testing, until someone makes a rock in a dark room.

So when you collect, think in two lists:

  • What should decide the class: the shape of the hand.
  • What shouldn't matter: lighting, angle, distance from the camera, position in the frame, background, which hand, whose hand, sleeves, and the camera itself.

For every item on the second list, record every class under several versions of it. Here's a coverage table for a rock-paper-scissors dataset, with sample counts for each class under each condition:

Read it like a map of what the model has seen. Every class has plenty of lamp-on, close-up samples, so it will do well there. But look at Lamp off: Paper has 25 samples and Rock has none. In a dim room, the model's best clue is "dim pictures are usually Paper," so a dim rock is likely to come out as Paper. The same thing happens with Left hand and 2nd person: only Paper has them, so any left hand starts to look like Paper.

The fix isn't more samples overall. It's filling the white cells, so that no condition belongs to just one class.

📝 Note

Sound and pose have their own "shouldn't matter" lists. For sound: distance from the mic, the room, background noise, and whose voice. For pose: the FAQ points out that the pose model tracks where you are in the frame as well as your body's shape, so standing on the left can look like a different pose than standing on the right. Record each pose in several spots.

#People in your data, and people who shouldn't be

Priya's brother is a privacy problem because he didn't agree. He's also a data problem: if he was behind her mostly during Left samples, the model may partly learn "brother in the background means Left." Before every recording session, write down:

  • Who will appear, and whether each person agreed after you told them what it's for and where it's kept.
  • Where you'll record, and what's visible behind you: people, screens, mail, photos.
  • What you'll do if someone asks to be removed: delete their samples, retrain, and save a new version.

⚠️ Watch out

Two recording habits that quietly ruin datasets.

  1. Recording each class in one long burst. All Rock in the first minute, all Paper in the second. Lighting drifts and you shift in your chair, so the model can learn the drift. Record the classes in turns, and change conditions between turns.
  2. Pressing record before the gesture is formed. The class fills up with half-made shapes that belong to no class. Make the gesture first, then press.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A sign-language helper has classes A, B, and J. The letter J is signed by drawing a hook in the air. What's the problem?

  • The number of classes is fine; Teachable Machine takes as many as you add.

  • A single frame of J looks like the start or end of the movement, which can resemble other hand shapes. Motions need a different kind of model, or a still pose that stands in for them.

  • Their hand shapes differ; the issue is that J depends on movement.

Show answer

B. A single frame of J looks like the start or end of the movement, which can resemble other hand shapes. Motions need a different kind of model, or a still pose that stands in for them.

2All of your Scissors samples were recorded in the afternoon; all of your Rock samples at night. Testing at night, the model says Rock for almost everything. Why?

  • Hand shape isn't the issue here; the model's scores are following the light, not the hand.

  • The model learns whatever differs between classes. Record both classes in both kinds of light so brightness stops being a clue.

  • More training would only learn the brightness shortcut more firmly.

Show answer

B. The model learns whatever differs between classes. Record both classes in both kinds of light so brightness stops being a clue.

3You have 25 samples in a class. How many does Teachable Machine hold back as test samples?

  • It always sets aside a share to check itself.

  • 15% of 25 is 3.75. With so few, the accuracy it reports for that class can swing wildly.

  • The split is 85% training and 15% test.

Show answer

B. 15% of 25 is 3.75. With so few, the accuracy it reports for that class can swing wildly.

4Which class set needs a Nothing class most?

  • Between rounds the camera sees no gesture at all, and without a Nothing class the model must still answer Rock, Paper, or Scissors.

  • If every photo always contains a banana, every input really does belong to one of the two classes.

  • Only audio projects come with a built-in Background Noise class. Image projects don't.

Show answer

A. Between rounds the camera sees no gesture at all, and without a Nothing class the model must still answer Rock, Paper, or Scissors.

Key takeaways

  • The model must split 100% across your classes for every input, so classes can't overlap and you need a "nothing" class when inputs can be empty.
  • Image models judge one frame at a time; choose classes a single still photo can separate.
  • Plan 50 to 150 image samples per class, with similar counts in every class. Audio needs at least 8 per class plus 20 seconds of background noise.
  • The model learns any difference between classes. Record every class under every lighting, angle, distance, background, and person you expect.
  • Record only people who agreed, and check the background before you press the button.

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): the "Tweaking your model" section suggests experiments with backgrounds, microphones, framing, and bias that match this lesson.
  • PAIR Explorables (opens in a new tab): interactive essays from Google's People + AI Research team on how data choices shape what models learn. Start with any one on fairness or bias.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a project idea into a written data plan: classes, definitions, conditions, and people.
  • Record four classes in short rotating sessions instead of one long burst per class.
  • Inspect thumbnails and remove half-formed or misfiled samples.
  • Run a quick smoke-test training and save the project as version 1.

You're going to build the dataset behind a rock, paper, scissors game that watches your hand through the webcam. By the end you'll have a saved project that looks like this, with every class recorded in every condition:

The goal of this build is the dataset, not the model. You'll train it properly and read its graphs in Module 3. A good model can't come out of a bad dataset, so this is where the real work is.

#Step 1: Write the data plan

Open your project log and write this before touching Teachable Machine. Three minutes of planning saves an hour of re-recording.

Notice that each class definition describes what the camera sees, not what you mean. "Paper: palm toward the camera" rules out a sideways flat hand, which looks a lot like a karate chop.

#Step 2: Create the project and the classes

  1. Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com, click Get Started, then Image Project, then Standard image model.
  2. Rename Class 1 to Rock and Class 2 to Paper with the pencil icons.
  3. Click Add a class twice, and name the new cards Scissors and Nothing.

Check the spelling now: class names travel with the model when you export it, and a game will later compare against those exact names.

#Step 3: Set up the scene

  • Put the laptop on a table, not your lap, so the camera doesn't bounce.
  • Check what's behind you in the webcam view. Move anything personal out of frame, and make sure nobody will walk through.
  • Have a lamp you can switch on and off. If you don't have one, use "curtains open" and "curtains closed," or "facing the window" and "back to the window."

#Step 4: Record round 1 (lamp on, close, right hand)

For each class in turn, click Webcam on its card and record a short burst of about 12 samples:

  1. Make the gesture first, then press and hold Hold to Record.
  2. While holding, rotate your wrist slightly and move your hand around the frame. Keep the gesture the same.
  3. Release after about half a second. At the default 24 frames a second, that gives roughly a dozen samples.

For Nothing, record a burst of the empty frame, one of your face with no hand up, and one with your hand moving in and out of view.

💡 Tip

If holding the button while posing is awkward, open the webcam's Settings, switch Hold to Record off, and set Delay to 2 and Duration to 1. Each click then gives you a two-second countdown and about a second of recording.

#Step 5: Rounds 2 to 8, changing one condition each time

Repeat the four-class round for every combination in the plan. Two lights, two distances, and two hands make eight rounds:

Round Light Distance Hand
1 on close right
2 on far right
3 on close left
4 on far left
5 off close right
6 off far right
7 off close left
8 off far left

Recording all four classes in each round is the key decision of this build. If you recorded all of Rock first and all of Scissors twenty minutes later, the light from the window would have changed between them, and the model could learn the time of day. Rotating means every class sees the same drift.

After eight rounds of about 12, each class has close to 100 samples. Each card shows its count, such as 96 Image Samples.

#Step 6: Clean the data

Scroll through each class's thumbnails. Click any thumbnail to open it larger, and look for:

  • Half-formed gestures: a fist that's halfway to a V belongs to no class. Delete it.
  • Misfiled samples: a Paper photo that ended up in Scissors. Use the viewer's option to move it to the right class.
  • Blurry frames where the hand is a smear. Delete a few; keep slightly blurry ones, since real play is blurry too.
  • Anything private that slipped into the background.

Then compare the counts. If one class is more than about 15 samples short of the others, record one more round for it in a condition it's thin on.

#Step 7: Smoke test

Click Train Model and stay on the tab until it reads Model Trained. Leave the Advanced settings alone for now.

In Preview, make each sign a few times, in both lights and with both hands. You're not grading the model yet, just checking that the dataset isn't broken. A healthy first result looks like:

Weaker scores far from the camera are normal, because a small hand gives the model fewer pixels to work with. A result where one class wins everything means something's wrong with the data: usually a class with far more samples, or a class recorded under different conditions from the rest.

#Step 8: Save version 1

  1. Open ☰ › Download project as file.
  2. Rename the file to rock-paper-scissors-v1- followed by today's date, and move it into your course folder.
  3. Add the actual counts and anything you noticed in the smoke test to your log:

That log entry and the .tm file are the finished product of this build.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why record all four classes in each round instead of finishing one class before starting the next?

  • If each class came from a different time, the light itself would differ between classes, and the model could learn that difference instead of hand shape.

  • You can record as long as you hold the button; the dozen is a choice that keeps rounds short.

  • The total number of samples is the same either way.

Show answer

A. If each class came from a different time, the light itself would differ between classes, and the model could learn that difference instead of hand shape.

2Your smoke test shows Scissors far from the camera scoring 60% Scissors and 35% Paper. What is the most useful next step?

  • Then the model couldn't recognize Paper at all.

  • Changing settings before looking at the data hides the cause. Module 3 covers settings.

  • The confusion is specific to one condition, so add data for that condition and check that nothing is mislabeled there.

Show answer

C. The confusion is specific to one condition, so add data for that condition and check that nothing is mislabeled there.

3Why does the Nothing class include your hand moving in and out of view?

  • You want similar counts in every class, not a bigger Nothing class.

  • Without them, a hand on its way into the frame would be forced into Rock, Paper, or Scissors.

Show answer

B. Without them, a hand on its way into the frame would be forced into Rock, Paper, or Scissors.

Key takeaways

  • Write the data plan first: class definitions in terms of what the camera sees, the conditions to cover, and who appears.
  • Record in rounds, all classes per round, changing one condition each time.
  • Clean thumbnails before training: remove half-formed gestures and move misfiled samples.
  • A smoke test checks the dataset, not the model. Save a versioned .tm file and a log entry when you're done.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add Lizard and Spock from the five-gesture version of the game. Do they pass the one-frame test against the existing classes?
  • With their agreement, record one round of a friend's hands, then test the v1 model on a second friend who isn't in the data.
  • Record only right-hand samples in a separate project and test it with your left hand. How much worse is it?

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): "Why isn't it working like I want it to?" lists changing backgrounds, framing, and confusing examples as experiments to try on your dataset.
  • Datasets: Data characteristics (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course page on what makes data reliable, including bad labels and duplicates.

What you'll learn

  • Spot overlapping classes and classes that need motion, and rewrite them.
  • Predict, then observe, how a missing "nothing" class changes a model's answers.
  • Create a background shortcut on purpose and fix it.
  • Find the gaps in a dataset's coverage, and write a consent plan for recording other people.

These exercises mix paper problems with real experiments in Teachable Machine. For each experiment, write your prediction in your log before you run it. The point isn't to guess right; it's to notice when your picture of the model is wrong.

Keep your rock-paper-scissors-v1 project handy. Exercises 2 and 4 use it.

#Warm-up: one frame or not?

For each pair, decide whether a single still photo is enough to tell the classes apart.

  1. Thumbs up / Thumbs down
  2. Clapping / Not clapping
  3. Sitting / Standing
  4. Nodding yes / Shaking head no
  5. Ripe banana / Green banana
Show solution

1, 3, and 5 work from one frame: the shapes or colors differ in a still photo. 2 and 4 are motions. A single frame of a clap is two hands near each other, which also happens when you're not clapping, and one frame of a nod is just a tilted head. For a sound model, though, clapping is easy: it's a distinctive one-second sound.

#Exercise 1: Repair a class list

A student's game controller has these classes: Left (arm pointing left), Right (arm pointing right), Jump (both arms up), Arms up, Move (any arm movement), and Wave. Rewrite the list so every class passes the one-frame test and no two overlap. Say what you removed and why.

Need a hint?

Look for one class that's just another name for another, one that contains several others, and one that needs motion.

Show solution
  • Arms up duplicates Jump (both describe both arms raised). Keep one.
  • Move contains Left, Right, and Jump, because they're all arm movements. Remove it.
  • Wave is a motion. Remove it, or replace it with a still pose such as "one hand on head."
  • Add Nothing for standing with arms down, which the game will see most of the time.

Final list: Left, Right, Jump, Nothing. Four classes, each a still pose, with no overlaps.

#Exercise 2: Take away the Nothing class

Open rock-paper-scissors-v1. On the Nothing card, open the ⋮ menu and choose Disable Class. Train, then point the camera at an empty wall.

Prediction first: what will the bars show for an empty wall?

Need a hint?

The model must split 100% across the classes that are switched on. Which of Rock, Paper, and Scissors looks most like a blank, evenly colored picture?

Show solution

Expected result: one of the three hand classes gets most of the bar, often above 80%, even though there's no hand at all. Which one varies from dataset to dataset; Paper is common because a flat palm is a large, even patch of color. The model isn't broken. It has no way to say "none," so it picks the closest option, and it often picks it confidently.

Use Enable Class to switch Nothing back on and train again: the empty wall goes back to Nothing at nearly 100%. Keep this result in mind for Module 4, because high confidence on something the model was never trained on is one of the main ways models fool people.

#Exercise 3: Build a background shortcut on purpose

Start a new image project with two classes, Pen and Spoon.

  1. Record about 40 Pen samples holding the pen in front of a plain wall.
  2. Record about 40 Spoon samples holding the spoon in front of something busy, like a bookshelf or a poster.
  3. Train. Test each object in front of its own background, then swap: hold the pen in front of the bookshelf.

Predict the swapped result before you test.

Need a hint?

What is the biggest difference between the two classes in your samples: the small object, or everything behind it?

Show solution

Expected result: in front of their own backgrounds, both objects score close to 100%. Swapped, the pen in front of the bookshelf is called Spoon, often with high confidence, and the spoon in front of the wall leans toward Pen. The background takes up most of each picture, so it's the easiest difference for the model to learn.

The fix: record 40 more samples of each object in front of both backgrounds, then train again. Now the background appears in both classes, so it stops being a clue, and the swapped test follows the object.

#Exercise 4: How few is too few?

Make a new image project with the same four classes as rock-paper-scissors, but record only 5 samples per class (a single quick tap of Hold to Record). Train it, and compare it side by side with your v1 model (open v1 in a second tab).

Move your hand slowly across the frame while holding Scissors. Count how many times the top class flips in ten seconds for each model.

Need a hint?

Five samples taken in a fraction of a second are nearly identical. What happens when your hand is somewhere none of the five were?

Show solution

Expected result: the 5-sample model flips often (several times in ten seconds), especially at the edges of the frame and when you change distance, and its winning scores bounce between about 50% and 95%. The v1 model stays on Scissors almost all the time. Yet the small model can look perfect by its own measure: with 5 samples per class, Teachable Machine holds back just 1 per class for testing, so its self-check rests on 4 photos taken a split second after the ones it trained on.

#Exercise 5: Find the gaps

A classmate recorded a recycling sorter and shares these counts:

Bright desk Dim room Held in hand On the table
Recycling 40 0 35 5
Trash 10 30 0 40
Nothing 20 20 0 40

List the two worst gaps and predict what the model will do in each situation.

Need a hint?

For each column, ask: is this condition shared by the classes, or does it belong mostly to one? A condition that belongs to one class becomes a clue for that class.

Show solution
  1. Dim room has no Recycling at all. A can photographed in a dim room will probably come out as Trash or Nothing, because to the model "dim" means "not Recycling."
  2. Held in hand has Recycling only. Anything held in a hand, including a banana peel, is likely to be called Recycling.

The chart below plots the same counts. The bars that are missing from a group are the gaps. The fix is to record Recycling in the dim room and on the table, and Trash in hand.

#Exercise 6: Write a consent plan

You want to make a pose model with five classmates at lunch so it works on more than one body. Write the short script you'll say to each person, and the three rules you'll follow with the data.

Need a hint?

Cover what you're recording, what it's for, where it's stored, who will see it, and how they can get out later.

Show solution

A good script: "I'm making a pose model for a class project. I'd like to record about 30 seconds of you doing four poses on my laptop camera. The pictures stay in a file on my computer and won't be posted anywhere. Only the trained model, which doesn't contain pictures, might be shared. You can say no, and if you change your mind later I'll delete your part. Is that okay?"

Rules: record only people who say yes, with nobody else in the background; keep the project file on your own computer, not in a shared folder; and if anyone asks to be removed, delete their samples, retrain, and save a new version. Write each person's yes in your log with the date.

#Challenge: A pose model that works anywhere in the frame

Start a Pose Project with classes Arms up, T pose, and Nothing (arms down). Record every sample standing in the center of the frame. Train, then test each pose standing at the far left and far right of the frame. Then fix it.

Need a hint?

The pose model tracks the positions of your body's key points, such as wrists and shoulders, within the picture. What changes about those positions when you step to one side, even if your pose is identical?

Show solution

Expected result: poses in the center score well. At the edges, scores drop and some poses get confused (often T pose with Nothing), because every key point has shifted sideways compared with the training samples. The Teachable Machine FAQ calls this out: the pose model tracks where you appear in the frame as well as your pose.

The fix is to record each class in three spots (left, center, right), and at two distances, then train again. Turning Hold to Record off in Settings with a 3-second Delay lets you click, step into place, and pose.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a model trained on lopsided data favors the biggest class, using accuracy.
  • Tell the difference between a balanced dataset and a representative one.
  • Describe what happens when you click Train Model: transfer learning, the 85/15 split, epochs, batches, and learning rate.
  • Read the Accuracy per epoch and Loss per epoch graphs, and spot overfitting.

Jordan records his rock, paper, scissors dataset in a hurry. He holds Hold to Record for twenty seconds on Rock and two seconds each on Paper and Scissors. He trains, opens the graphs, and sees accuracy climb past 90%. Then he plays a round: Rock. Paper? Rock. Scissors? Rock, at 70%.

Ninety percent accurate and nearly useless. Both are true, and the reason is the most common trap in machine learning.

#A model that always says Rock is 83% accurate

Here are Jordan's sample counts, and what a "model" that ignores the picture and always answers Rock would score:

Look at the last printed line. Accuracy is the share of samples the model gets right, and it counts every sample equally. When 83% of the samples are Rock, answering Rock is a very good strategy for scoring well, even though it never recognizes a single paper.

Training is a search for settings that make fewer mistakes overall. In Jordan's data, a mistake on Paper costs the model the same as a mistake on Rock, but there are ten times fewer chances to make it. So the search leans hard toward Rock. When the model is unsure, Rock is its safest bet, and you see that as the Rock bar winning every close call.

The fix is in the data, not the settings: give every class a similar number of samples. Either record more Paper and Scissors (best, since you also add variety), or delete Rock samples until the counts are close.

#Balanced is not the same as representative

A balanced dataset has similar counts in every class. A representative one covers the situations the model will actually face: every lighting, distance, hand, and background from Module 2. You need both.

Here's a dataset that's perfectly balanced and still broken: 100 Rock, 100 Paper, 100 Scissors, all recorded with your right hand. It will struggle with every left hand, equally across all three classes.

And here's a subtle one. In a real game, the camera sees Nothing far more often than any sign. Should Nothing get extra samples to match? No. Extra samples teach the model that Nothing is usually the right answer, so it will lean toward Nothing whenever a sign is a bit unclear. Keep the counts similar, and handle "the camera mostly sees nothing" in the game's logic later.

⚠️ Watch out

Ways datasets become lopsided without you noticing.

  • Holding the record button longer for one class. At about 24 frames a second, three extra seconds is 70 extra samples.
  • Adding a class late and recording it in a single quick burst.
  • Deleting bad frames from one class and not re-recording.

Check the counts on every class card before every training run. Within about 10% of each other is a good target.

#What happens when you click Train Model

Teachable Machine doesn't build a model from scratch. It uses transfer learning: a network called MobileNet, already trained on a huge collection of photos, turns each of your images into a long list of numbers describing its shapes, edges, and textures. Then Teachable Machine trains a small final layer that learns which patterns in those numbers go with which of your classes.

Before training, Teachable Machine sets aside 15% of each class as test samples. They're never used for learning; after each round of training, the model is checked on them to see how it does on pictures it didn't learn from.

The Advanced section under Train Model has three settings that control the training itself.

Epochs (default 50 for image projects). One epoch means every training sample has gone through the model once. With 50 epochs, the model works through your whole training set 50 times, improving a little each pass.

Batch Size (default 16; the menu offers 16 up to 512). The model doesn't adjust itself after every single sample. It looks at a batch, works out how it should change, and adjusts once. Teachable Machine's own example: with 80 images and a batch size of 16, there are 80 ÷ 16 = 5 batches, and after all 5, one epoch is done. Step through it here:

Watch updates climb by one per batch: 5 adjustments per epoch, 10 after two epochs. At the default 50 epochs, that's 250 adjustments.

Learning Rate (default 0.001 for image projects). How big each adjustment is. Too big, and the model overshoots and its accuracy jumps around; too small, and it barely moves in 50 epochs. Teachable Machine's tooltip warns that even small changes here have huge effects. Leave it alone unless an experiment calls for it, and use Reset Defaults to put all three back.

#Reading the graphs under the hood

In the Advanced section, click Under the hood. A panel opens with two line graphs that fill in as training runs, one point per epoch:

  • Accuracy per epoch: acc (on training samples) and test acc (on the 15% test samples). 1.0 means every sample right.
  • Loss per epoch: loss and test loss. Loss also counts how confident the right answers are. A correct answer at 60% confidence has more loss than a correct answer at 90%, so loss keeps falling after accuracy hits 1.0. Zero is perfect.

Here's a typical pair of graphs for a dataset like the one you built in Module 2:

What to read from it:

  1. Both curves rise fast, then flatten. Most learning happens in the first 10 to 15 epochs. More epochs mostly polish.
  2. There's a gap at the end: training accuracy reaches 1.0, test accuracy settles near 0.92. Some gap is normal. The model has studied the training samples and is only meeting the test ones.
  3. Test loss bottoms out around epoch 20, then creeps up while training loss keeps falling. That's the signature of overfitting, which Teachable Machine defines as learning the training samples so closely that the model does worse on the test samples. It's memorizing details of your training photos that don't carry over.

The opposite, underfitting, looks like both curves stuck low: the model hasn't captured the difference between classes. With Teachable Machine that usually means classes that look too alike, too few samples, or a learning rate that's been changed.

📝 Note

Test accuracy is checked on frames from the same sessions you trained on, often a split second apart from training frames. That makes it optimistic. A model with 0.95 test accuracy can still fail in a new room. Module 4 is about testing on truly new examples.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A dataset has 300 Nothing samples, 100 Rock, 100 Paper, and 100 Scissors. What accuracy does a model get by always answering Nothing?

  • That would be true if the classes were equal in size. Accuracy counts samples, not classes.

  • 300 of the 600 samples are Nothing, so always guessing Nothing is right half the time without looking at the picture.

  • Only 300 of 600 samples are Nothing.

Show answer

B. 300 of the 600 samples are Nothing, so always guessing Nothing is right half the time without looking at the picture.

2You have 120 training samples and a batch size of 16. About how many adjustments does the model make in one epoch?

  • 16 is the batch size, the number of samples in each batch.

  • 120 ÷ 16 is 7.5, so there are 7 full batches and one smaller batch of 8: 8 adjustments per epoch.

  • That would be a batch size of 1, where the model adjusts after every sample.

Show answer

B. 120 ÷ 16 is 7.5, so there are 7 full batches and one smaller batch of 8: 8 adjustments per epoch.

3Under the hood, training accuracy is 1.0 and test accuracy is 0.55. What does that tell you?

  • Test accuracy is the better guide to new data, and 0.55 is poor.

  • A large gap is overfitting, or a sign that the test samples differ from the training ones. Look at the data first: variety, balance, and mislabeled samples.

  • A learning rate that's too small would keep training accuracy low too.

Show answer

B. A large gap is overfitting, or a sign that the test samples differ from the training ones. Look at the data first: variety, balance, and mislabeled samples.

4Jordan's model says Rock for every close call. What's the best first fix?

  • More training on lopsided data learns the lean more firmly.

  • The lean comes from the data, so changing step size doesn't remove it.

  • Balancing removes the reason to favor Rock, and the new samples add variety at the same time.

Show answer

C. Balancing removes the reason to favor Rock, and the new samples add variety at the same time.

Key takeaways

  • Accuracy counts samples, so a class with far more samples can earn high accuracy by itself. Keep class counts within about 10% of each other.
  • Balanced (similar counts) and representative (covers real conditions) are separate goals; you need both.
  • Teachable Machine trains only the last layer on top of MobileNet, holding back 15% of each class as test samples.
  • An epoch is one pass over the training samples; a batch is how many samples go by before each adjustment; the learning rate is the size of each adjustment. Defaults for images: 50, 16, 0.001.
  • In the graphs, a growing gap between training and test curves, or test loss rising, means overfitting.

#Further reading

  • Datasets: Class-imbalanced datasets (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course on why imbalance hurts and how experts rebalance.
  • Overfitting: Interpreting loss curves (opens in a new tab): a gallery of real loss curves with what each shape means.
  • Linear regression: Hyperparameters (opens in a new tab): epochs, batch size, and learning rate explained with small examples. The math is optional; the ideas are the same ones in Teachable Machine's Advanced panel.

What you'll learn

  • Train with Under the hood open and describe what the accuracy and loss graphs show.
  • Use Calculate accuracy per class and Calculate confusion matrix to find the weakest class.
  • Watch what a ten-to-one imbalance does to close calls in the preview.
  • Make one targeted, balanced change to the data, retrain, and compare versions in a log.

Last module you built rock-paper-scissors-v1. Now you'll train it properly, find out exactly where it's weak, break it on purpose with lopsided data, and end with a better version 2. The finished product is this comparison in your project log:

Your numbers will differ. What matters is the pattern, and that you can explain every cell.

#Step 1: Reopen version 1 and check the counts

  1. Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com, click Get Started, then Open an existing project from a file, and choose your rock-paper-scissors-v1 file.
  2. Read the sample count on each class card, and write the four numbers in your log.

If any class is more than about 10% smaller than the largest, record one more varied round for it before going on. Training on unbalanced counts would muddy everything that follows.

#Step 2: Train with the graphs open

  1. Under Train Model, open Advanced. Check the defaults: Epochs 50, Batch Size 16, Learning Rate 0.001. If anything else shows, click Reset Defaults.
  2. Click Under the hood. A panel opens; until you train, it says to train a model to see more detailed information.
  3. Click Train Model and watch. Stay on the tab.

The two graphs fill in one epoch at a time. On a clean four-class dataset you should see something like this: acc and test acc shoot up within the first 10 epochs and level off near the top; loss and test loss drop steeply, then flatten, with test loss staying a little above training loss.

Write the final test acc in your log: read it off the accuracy graph where the orange line ends.

#Step 3: Find the weakest class

Overall accuracy hides which class is struggling. Under the graphs, click Calculate accuracy per class and then Calculate confusion matrix. Both are worked out on the test samples, the 15% the model never trained on.

The confusion matrix is a grid: each row is the true class of the test samples, and each column is what the model predicted. Correct answers sit on the diagonal. Anything off the diagonal is a mix-up, and its position tells you which two classes are being confused. Here's what one might look like, with roughly 15 test samples per class:

Read the third row: of 15 Scissors test samples, 12 were right and 3 were called Paper. That's the weakest spot. To find out which Scissors samples, test in Preview: make Scissors close, far, in each light, with each hand, and note where the Paper bar grows. In most webcam datasets it's far away, where two fingers become a few pixels wide.

Write the weak class and the condition in your log.

#Step 4: Break it on purpose with lopsided data

Before fixing anything, see what imbalance does. You'll undo this in a minute, so make sure v1 is saved.

  1. On the Rock card, click Webcam and record about 300 more Rock samples (around 12 to 15 seconds of holding), moving your hand as usual.
  2. Check the card: Rock now has about four times the samples of each other class.
  3. Train again with Under the hood open, and calculate accuracy per class.

The graphs may look as good as before or even better, since a big share of the test samples are now easy Rock frames. The damage shows up in the Preview, on hard cases. Hold Scissors far away, form Paper slowly, or dim the light: close calls now tip to Rock. Hand halfway into the frame? Rock.

The extra Rock samples bought a few points on Rock and cost far more on the other two. Nothing about the hand shapes changed; the model simply learned that Rock is usually the right answer.

Now undo it: open ☰ › Open project from file and choose the v1 file again. Don't save the lopsided version.

#Step 5: Make one targeted, balanced fix

Back on v1, fix the weak spot you found in Step 3. If it was Scissors far away:

  1. Record a far-away round for Scissors, about 12 samples, with deliberate variety: both hands, both lights, fingers spread wide and narrow.
  2. Record a far-away round for every other class too, about the same size.

Step 2 of the fix is the one people skip. Adding samples only to Scissors fixes Scissors and quietly unbalances the dataset. Adding a round to every class keeps the counts close and teaches the model what all four classes look like far away, which is exactly where it was guessing.

Check the counts on the cards and write them in the log.

#Step 6: Retrain and compare

Train with Under the hood open, calculate accuracy per class and the confusion matrix, and test the weak case in Preview again. Fill in the v2 column of your comparison. Expect the Scissors-as-Paper cell of the confusion matrix to shrink, and far-away Scissors to win more often in the preview. If it didn't improve, the cause may be different from the one you guessed: look again at which thumbnails are in the Paper class, and whether any are mislabeled.

#Step 7: Save version 2

Open ☰ › Download project as file, rename it rock-paper-scissors-v2- plus the date, and finish the log entry: counts, settings (50 / 16 / 0.001), final test accuracy, the per-class result for your weak class, and one sentence on what changed. That entry, next to v1's, is the finished build.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1In Step 4, the overall test accuracy went up after adding 300 Rock samples, yet the model got worse in the preview. How?

  • Accuracy averages over samples. Adding many easy samples of one class lifts the average even as the other classes suffer.

  • The graphs are calculated correctly; they just answer a different question from "does it work on hard cases?"

  • Adding varied samples to every class usually helps. The problem was adding them to one class only.

Show answer

A. Accuracy averages over samples. Adding many easy samples of one class lifts the average even as the other classes suffer.

2Why add a far-away round to every class instead of only to Scissors?

  • It will train on any counts; equal counts are your choice.

  • If only Scissors had far-away samples, "far away" itself would become a clue for Scissors.

  • Each sample counts the same in training; what matters is covering the conditions for every class.

Show answer

B. If only Scissors had far-away samples, "far away" itself would become a clue for Scissors.

3In a confusion matrix, where do you look to see how often Paper was mistaken for Nothing?

  • That cell counts Nothing samples predicted as Paper, the opposite mistake.

  • Rows are the true class and columns are the prediction, so this cell counts Paper samples the model called Nothing.

Show answer

B. Rows are the true class and columns are the prediction, so this cell counts Paper samples the model called Nothing.

Key takeaways

  • Open Advanced › Under the hood before training to watch accuracy and loss per epoch, then calculate per-class accuracy and the confusion matrix.
  • Overall accuracy can rise while the model gets worse on the cases you care about; per-class results and preview tests show what the average hides.
  • Extra samples in one class make close calls tip toward that class.
  • Fix weaknesses with a targeted round in every class, so the counts stay balanced, then compare versions in your log.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Train v2 with Epochs set to 10, then 100, and compare the shape of the curves with the default 50.
  • Ask a friend (who agrees to it) to try the model. Which class fails first on a hand that isn't in the data?
  • Add a fifth class, Thumbs up, with the same number of samples as the others. Does it get confused with Rock?

#Further reading

  • Datasets: Class-imbalanced datasets (opens in a new tab): how imbalance shows up in real projects and the standard ways to rebalance.
  • Classification: Accuracy, recall, precision (opens in a new tab): why accuracy alone can mislead, with a confusion-matrix walkthrough. You'll meet these ideas again in Module 5.

m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Calculate the accuracy a "always pick the biggest class" model gets, and explain why it misleads.
  • Count batches per epoch and total adjustments from the training settings.
  • Recognize underfitting, a healthy fit, and overfitting from accuracy and loss curves.
  • Run and explain experiments that change epochs, learning rate, and class balance.

Use your rock-paper-scissors-v2 project for the Teachable Machine experiments. Before each one, write a prediction in your log. After each one, click Reset Defaults in the Advanced panel so the next experiment starts clean (Epochs 50, Batch Size 16, Learning Rate 0.001).

#Warm-up

A dataset has 50 Cat, 50 Dog, and 250 Rabbit samples. What accuracy does a model get if it answers Rabbit for everything?

Show solution

250 out of 350 samples are Rabbit, so it scores 250 ÷ 350 ≈ 71% without looking at a single picture. Any accuracy you see for this dataset should be compared with 71%, not with 0%.

#Exercise 1: The baseline for three datasets

For each dataset, calculate the "always pick the biggest class" accuracy, and say which dataset's 90% accuracy would impress you most.

Dataset Counts
A Rock 100, Paper 100, Scissors 100
B Recycling 40, Trash 360
C Clap 30, Snap 30, Whistle 30, Background Noise 210
Need a hint?

Divide the biggest class by the total. A 90% model is only impressive when 90% is far above that baseline.

Show solution

A 90% model on A is far above its 33% baseline, so it's genuinely learning. On B it is no better than always saying Trash, which also scores 90%. On C it beats the 70% baseline, but much of its score may come from Background Noise. Dataset A's 90% is the most impressive.

#Exercise 2: Count the adjustments

You have 200 training samples. How many batches are in one epoch, and how many adjustments does training make in total, for each of these settings?

  1. Batch Size 16, Epochs 50
  2. Batch Size 32, Epochs 50
  3. Batch Size 16, Epochs 10
Need a hint?

Batches per epoch is samples ÷ batch size, rounded up, because a leftover partial batch still counts. Total adjustments is batches per epoch × epochs.

Show solution
  1. 200 ÷ 16 = 12.5, so 13 batches per epoch (12 full, one of 8) and 13 × 50 = 650 adjustments.
  2. 200 ÷ 32 = 6.25, so 7 batches per epoch and 350 adjustments.
  3. 13 batches per epoch and 13 × 10 = 130 adjustments.

Bigger batches mean fewer, smoother adjustments per epoch. That's why Teachable Machine's tooltip says you probably won't need to change batch size: epochs have a much bigger effect.

#Exercise 3: Diagnose three training runs

The graphs below show test accuracy and test loss for three made-up training runs. Label each run as underfitting, a healthy fit, or overfitting, and give the clue.

Need a hint?

Underfitting: never gets good. Overfitting: gets good, then gets worse on the test samples. Healthy: gets good and stays there.

Show solution
  • Run A: underfitting. Test accuracy never climbs past about 0.5 and loss barely falls. The model hasn't found the difference between classes. Check for classes that look alike, too few samples, or a learning rate that was made tiny.
  • Run B: healthy. Fast rise, then flat; loss falls and stays low.
  • Run C: overfitting. Test loss bottoms out around epoch 15, then climbs, and test accuracy sags slightly. The model is fitting details of the training samples that don't carry over. More varied data helps more than fewer epochs, but for this run 15 to 20 epochs would also have done better than 50.

#Exercise 4: Too few and too many epochs

In rock-paper-scissors-v2, open Advanced and Under the hood. Train three times, with Epochs set to 3, then 50, then 300. Each time, note the final test acc, the shape of the curves, and how confident the preview is on a far-away Scissors.

Need a hint?

Most of the learning in the curves you've seen happens in the first 10 to 15 epochs. What does stopping at 3 cut off? What can 250 extra epochs add?

Show solution

Expected results (your numbers will vary):

  • 3 epochs: the curves are three points that stop while still rising steeply. Test accuracy is often a few points lower, and the preview bars are less decisive: the winning class might show 60% to 80% where it showed 95%.
  • 50 epochs: curves rise and flatten, as in the build.
  • 300 epochs: training takes several times longer. Training loss keeps inching toward zero, test accuracy barely changes, and test loss may start drifting up. The preview looks about the same as 50, perhaps a little more extreme in its percentages.

Conclusion: past the point where the curves flatten, extra epochs cost time and invite overfitting without improving the model. Click Reset Defaults when you're done.

#Exercise 5: Learning rate too big and too small

Train v2 twice more: once with Learning Rate set to 0.1 (100 times the default), and once with 0.00001 (100 times smaller). Keep the graphs open.

Need a hint?

The learning rate is the size of each adjustment. Picture walking downhill in fog with giant leaps versus tiny shuffles.

Show solution
  • 0.1: the curves are jagged. Accuracy jumps up and down between epochs, and loss may spike instead of falling smoothly. The preview can be erratic, flipping between classes or showing 100% for the wrong one. Each step is so large it overshoots good settings.
  • 0.00001: the curves crawl. After 50 epochs test accuracy may still be well below the default run, and the preview's top bar is often split, like 55% and 40%. The model hasn't moved far enough.

This is why the tooltip says "Be careful tweaking this number!" Click Reset Defaults afterward.

#Exercise 6: Choose how to rebalance

A classmate's counts are Rock 150, Paper 60, Scissors 90, Nothing 100. They want balance and have time for one more 15-minute recording session. Write a plan, and explain what goes wrong if they simply delete samples until every class has 60.

Need a hint?

Deleting is quick, but what does it throw away? And which classes most need new conditions, not just more of the same?

Show solution

Deleting down to 60 each throws away 160 samples, and with them much of the variety in Rock, Scissors, and Nothing. Each class would also keep only 9 test samples (15% of 60, rounded up), so the per-class accuracy becomes jumpy.

A better plan for one session: record about 40 new Paper and 10 new Scissors samples in conditions they're missing (check their thumbnails for which lights, distances, and hands are thin). Then delete about 50 of the most repetitive Rock frames, which are usually long runs of near-identical thumbnails. Result: roughly 100 per class, with more variety than before.

#Challenge: When a lean is on purpose

In a game, a wrong move is worse than no move. A classmate suggests giving Nothing three times as many samples as each sign, so the model "plays it safe." Train a copy of v2 that way (record about 200 extra Nothing samples), test it, and decide whether you agree.

Need a hint?

Test half-formed gestures and far-away signs. Then ask whether a cleaner way exists to get "don't act unless sure" without changing the data.

Show solution

Expected result: close calls now go to Nothing. Clear, close-up signs still work, but far-away and slightly sloppy signs are often ignored. So the classmate gets what they wanted: fewer wrong moves, and more missed moves.

The catch is that you can't control how far it leans; it's set by the counts. A cleaner method is to keep the data balanced and let the game decide: act only when the top class's confidence is above a threshold, such as 80%. You'll see confidence properly in Module 4 and use thresholds in a game later in the course. Delete the copy; keep v2.
