m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain how the preview's percentages are made and why they always add up to 100%.
  • Give three reasons a model can show 99% and still be wrong.
  • Explain why Teachable Machine's own test samples flatter a model.
  • Plan an unseen test that covers new people, places, lighting, and objects.

Your rock, paper, scissors model reports a test accuracy of 0.97. You take the laptop to the kitchen, make a fist under the yellow ceiling light, and the preview says Scissors 99%. Back at your desk it's Rock 100% again.

Nothing is broken. The 0.97 and the 99% are both honest numbers. They just answer narrower questions than the ones you were asking, and this module is about reading them for what they are.

#Where the percentages come from

For every frame, the model computes a raw score for each class: a number that's higher the more the picture matches what it learned for that class. Scores can be any size, even negative. To show them as bars, Teachable Machine converts them so they're all positive and add up to 100%. The conversion (called softmax) exaggerates differences: a class whose score is a little ahead gets a much bigger share. Step through it with made-up scores:

Rock's score is only 2.5 points above Paper's, but it ends up with about 88% of the bar. Notice what you can't see in the result: whether the scores were all large or all small. A strong match and a weak match can produce the same 88%, as long as the gap between classes is the same.

So the precise meaning of a confidence bar is: how strongly the model prefers this class over the other classes you gave it. It is not "the chance the model is right." Those can be close on pictures like the training data, and far apart on anything else.

#Three ways to be 99% sure and wrong

1. The answer isn't on the menu. Show your rock, paper, scissors model a coffee mug. The bars must still add up to 100% across Rock, Paper, Scissors, and Nothing. If the mug resembles Paper more than the others, Paper can take 99%. The model is extremely sure that, of the four options, Paper is the closest. It has no way to say "none of these."

2. The picture is outside what it learned. Your training samples covered your desk, your lamp, and your hands. A kitchen under yellow light shifts the colors and shadows of the whole picture. The model's scores for a frame like that are pushed around by features it never had a chance to learn about, and the push can land deep in one class's territory. Far from the training data, a large gap between scores is just as likely as a small one, so the confidence stops being informative.

3. It's been trained to be extreme. Loss rewards confident right answers, so training pushes the model to give big gaps on the training samples. A model trained for many epochs on near-identical frames learns to produce big gaps on almost anything. High confidence becomes a habit, not a judgment.

Here's what confidence looks like when a model meets photos it has never seen. Each dot is one unseen test photo: how confident the top answer was, and whether it was right.

The blue dots, right answers, sit mostly near the top of the scale, which is what you'd hope. But look at the orange ones. Four of the nine mistakes came with more than 90% confidence. If you only trusted answers above 90%, you'd still have been fooled four times. Low confidence is a useful warning; high confidence is not a guarantee.

#Why the built-in test is too easy

In Module 3 you read test acc from the graphs under the hood. Those test samples are a random 15% of your own recordings, so they were taken in the same room, same light, same hand, often a fraction of a second after a training frame. Testing on them is like studying from a practice quiz and then taking the same quiz with the questions reshuffled.

Real use is different, so here's how accuracy typically falls as tests get further from the training sessions:

The blue bars are the tests people usually run, and the orange bars are the ones that predict how the model behaves for someone else. An unseen example means one the model wasn't trained on and that wasn't recorded in the same session as the training data. The orange bars are where you learn something.

#Plan an unseen test

A good unseen test is planned before you see any results, so you can't steer it toward the answers you want.

  1. Decide what will change in real use. People, rooms, lighting, distance, camera, and for objects, different brands and shapes than the ones you trained on.
  2. Collect at least 10 examples per class, spread across those changes. Ten isn't many, but it's enough to see a pattern and few enough to finish.
  3. Write down the true class of each example before testing it. File names do this for you: r01.jpg is a rock.
  4. Record the top class and its confidence for every example, right or wrong.
  5. Never move a test photo into a class. The moment you train on it, it stops being unseen, and you lose your ruler for measuring the next version.

Anyone who appears in the test needs to have agreed, just as for training. Testing with other people's hands is the single most useful test you can run, which makes asking properly worth the effort.

⚠️ Watch out

Four mistakes that make a model look better than it is.

  1. Testing on the training objects. For a recycling sorter, if the test can is the same can you trained on, you've tested its memory, not its skill. Keep separate test objects.
  2. Testing only yourself, at your desk. That's the blue bars above.
  3. Reading one frame. In the live preview, bars jump between frames. Watch for a second or two; a sign that flickers between 95% Paper and 70% Scissors is an unsure answer, whatever any single frame says.
  4. "Fixing" the test. Deleting the test photos the model gets wrong, or adding them to training, makes the next score meaningless.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The preview shows Paper 99% when you hold up a coffee mug to your rock, paper, scissors model. What does the 99% mean?

  • The bars aren't the chance of being right; the model has no idea what a mug is.

  • The bars always split 100% across your classes. A mug that resembles Paper more than the others can take nearly all of it.

  • It was never trained on mugs. It's forced to pick the closest of its four options.

Show answer

B. The bars always split 100% across your classes. A mug that resembles Paper more than the others can take nearly all of it.

2Two raw scores are Rock 6.0 and Paper 3.5 for one frame, and Rock 1.0 and Paper -1.5 for another. Ignoring the other classes, how do the Rock bars compare?

  • Softmax depends on the gaps between scores, not their size.

  • The same gap gives the same split, which is why the bar can't tell you whether the match was strong or weak.

  • A negative score only matters relative to the others; the gap is what counts.

Show answer

B. The same gap gives the same split, which is why the bar can't tell you whether the match was strong or weak.

3Your model gets 97% on its built-in test samples and 60% on photos from a friend's house. Which number should you report to someone who'll use it at their house?

  • The built-in test samples came from your own sessions, so they flatter the model.

  • The unseen test is the better prediction of how it behaves somewhere new, and saying where it was measured keeps the number honest.

  • Averaging two different tests hides what each one tells you.

Show answer

B. The unseen test is the better prediction of how it behaves somewhere new, and saying where it was measured keeps the number honest.

4After your unseen test, three photos were wrong. A teammate suggests adding them to the training classes and testing again. What's the problem?

  • It can; that's exactly why the temptation exists.

  • The model would get those three right because it trained on them. Fix the data gap with new examples like them, and keep the test set untouched.

  • Every error is worth investigating; the issue is reusing the test photos for training.

Show answer

B. The model would get those three right because it trained on them. Fix the data gap with new examples like them, and keep the test set untouched.

Key takeaways

  • The bars come from scores converted to shares of 100% (softmax). They show how strongly the model prefers one of your classes over the others, not the chance it's right.
  • A model can be 99% sure and wrong when the right answer isn't a class, when the input is unlike its training data, or when training has made it habitually extreme.
  • Teachable Machine's built-in test samples come from your own recording sessions, so they overestimate how the model does elsewhere.
  • Plan unseen tests in advance, with new people, places, lighting, and objects, at least 10 per class, and never train on them.

#Further reading

  • Datasets: Dividing the original dataset (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course on training, validation, and test sets, and why test data must stay untouched.
  • Overfitting: Generalization (opens in a new tab): the reading that goes with this lesson's video, with conditions a test set must meet.
  • People + AI Guidebook: Explainability + Trust (opens in a new tab): how designers decide when to show confidence to users, and how to say it so people don't over-trust it.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Plan a 40-photo unseen test set that covers new rooms, lighting, and people.
  • Take and name the photos outside Teachable Machine, so they can never leak into training.
  • Test each photo through the preview's File input and fill in a test sheet with confidence.
  • Summarize the sheet: accuracy per class, confidence when right and wrong, and the confident mistakes.

So far you've judged your rock, paper, scissors model by its own graphs and by playing with it at your desk. Both are familiar tests. In this build you'll make the ruler you'll use for the rest of the course: a folder of 40 photos the model has never seen, and a test sheet of how it does on them. Here's the end result:

The gap between those two lines is the most useful number your model has produced so far.

#Step 1: Plan the photos

Each class gets 10 photos, spread across things that changed nowhere in your training data. Write the plan in your log first:

The last three Nothing photos test the "not on the menu" problem from the Notes: the correct answer is Nothing, but the model has never seen a mug.

No one to borrow a hand from? Use your other hand with a long sleeve, at a distance you didn't train on. It's a weaker test than a new person, and your log should say so.

#Step 2: Take the photos outside Teachable Machine

Use your computer's ordinary camera app, not Teachable Machine. Taking the photos somewhere else means they can't end up in a class by accident.

Windows

Press Start, type Camera, and open the Camera app. Click the photo button for each picture. Photos are saved in Pictures › Camera Roll.

macOS

Open Photo Booth from Applications and click the red camera button for each picture. To get the files out, select the photos and drag them from Photo Booth into a Finder folder.

Chromebook

Open the Camera app from the Launcher and take each photo. They're saved in the Files app under My files › Camera.

A phone works too, and a different camera is a good extra test. iPhones save HEIC files by default, which Teachable Machine won't accept; switch Settings › Camera › Formats to Most Compatible to get JPGs, or convert the files before testing.

#Step 3: Name and file them

Make a folder called test-set inside your course folder and rename each photo by its true class and a number: r01.jpg to r10.jpg for Rock, p01 to p10 for Paper, s01 to s10 for Scissors, and n01 to n10 for Nothing.

The name records the right answer, so you decide the truth before the model sees anything. Write one line per photo in your log saying what's in it ("s04: kitchen, sister's hand, fingers wide"), while you still remember.

⚠️ Watch out

This folder never goes into a class. Not one photo, not even to fix a mistake. The moment the model trains on a test photo, that photo measures memory instead of skill, and you can't compare versions fairly any more. If a photo shows a gap in the data, collect new examples like it for training.

#Step 4: Retrain version 2

Open rock-paper-scissors-v2 from your file (Get Started › Open an existing project from a file) and click Train Model with the default settings. Don't change any samples today; you're measuring v2 as it is.

#Step 5: Run the familiar test first

For comparison, do a quick live test at your usual desk: make each sign 10 times (Nothing means hand down), and tally how many times the top bar is the right class. Watch for a second each time rather than reading one frame. This is the blue-bar kind of test from the Notes, and it should score high.

#Step 6: Run the unseen test

  1. In the Preview panel, use the menu beside Input to switch from Webcam to File.
  2. Drag r01.jpg into the file area (or click it to choose the file). The bars show the model's answer for that photo.
  3. On your test sheet, write the photo, its true class, the top class, and that class's percentage. If it's wrong, add what you notice.
  4. Repeat for all 40.

Write the confidence for right answers too. You need both to see whether confidence tells right from wrong.

#Step 7: Summarize the sheet

You can do the tallies by hand. Here's an example sheet summarized, so you can see what to calculate and how to read it:

How to read it:

  • Unseen accuracy is 78%, against 95% at the desk. That drop is the honest size of the model's blind spots.
  • Scissors is the weak class. Three of its four mistakes went to Paper, the same mix-up the confusion matrix hinted at in Module 3, now measured on photos the model never saw.
  • Confidence helps, a little. Wrong answers averaged lower confidence than right ones. But four mistakes were at 93% or more, so a high bar alone can't be trusted.
  • Look at where the confident mistakes happened: a new person's hand (r08, s02), new light (s07), and an object that isn't a class (n03). Those are three different data problems, and each needs a different fix.

#Step 8: Log it and keep the set safe

Add the results to your project log: familiar score, unseen score, per-class results, the confident mistakes with their notes, and your best guess at the cause of each. Then copy the test-set folder somewhere safe. Every future version of this model will be measured on the same 40 photos, which is the only way to know whether a change helped.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why take the test photos with a separate camera app instead of recording them in Teachable Machine?

  • Quality isn't the reason; it's about keeping test and training data apart.

  • Photos recorded into a class become training data. A separate folder of files is much harder to mix up.

  • The preview tests live webcam frames too; the file input lets you test the same saved photos on every version.

Show answer

B. Photos recorded into a class become training data. A separate folder of files is much harder to mix up.

2Photo n03 (holding a mug) came back Paper 99%. Which fix fits this mistake?

  • That would spoil the test set. The photo would no longer be unseen.

  • The model has never been shown that objects aren't signs. New training examples like n03, but not n03 itself, fill the gap.

  • People will hold things in front of the camera. Keeping hard cases in the test is what makes it useful.

Show answer

B. The model has never been shown that objects aren't signs. New training examples like n03, but not n03 itself, fill the gap.

3Why test the same 40 photos on every future version of the model?

  • If the test set changed between versions, you couldn't tell whether the model improved or the photos got easier.

  • It doesn't keep anything about preview tests.

Show answer

A. If the test set changed between versions, you couldn't tell whether the model improved or the photos got easier.

Key takeaways

  • An unseen test set is a separate folder of photos from new rooms, light, and people, named by their true class before testing.
  • Never put a test photo into a class; collect new training examples like it instead.
  • Record both the answer and its confidence for every photo, right or wrong.
  • The gap between the familiar and unseen scores, and the list of confident mistakes, tell you what the model really can't do.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Test the same photos on your v1 project. Did the targeted fix from Module 3 help on unseen photos, or only on your desk?
  • Take 10 more photos of each sign with a phone camera, and compare the score with your laptop photos.
  • Sort the wrong answers by their notes (new person, new light, new object) and count which cause appears most.

#Further reading

  • Datasets: Dividing the original dataset (opens in a new tab): why test data must never influence training, explained with examples of how it leaks.
  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): "Why isn't it working like I want it to?" suggests testing against new backgrounds, lighting, and people, and tricking the model with a photo or drawing of an object.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Decide which preview readings to trust, and predict bars from raw scores.
  • Build a small recycling sorter with test items set aside before training.
  • Measure how confidence and accuracy change on held-out objects and new surfaces.
  • Choose a confidence threshold from test results, and say what it costs.

The middle exercises build a quick recycling sorter. Before you start, gather about a dozen clean, empty household items: cans, plastic bottles, a cardboard box, paper, and non-recyclable things like a chip bag, a candy wrapper, or a used paper towel. Recycling rules differ from town to town, so decide which items count as Recycling using your local program's list, and write that rule in your log. Wash anything that held food.

#Warm-up: which readings would you trust?

Three moments from a rock, paper, scissors preview. For each, would you act on the answer?

  1. Rock 51%, Paper 47%, steady for two seconds.
  2. Paper 99%, steady, for a flat hand at your desk.
  3. Flickering between Scissors 95% and Paper 80% several times a second.
Show solution
  1. No. A near tie means the model can't separate the two classes for this input. Treat it as "unsure."
  2. Yes, probably. It's steady, it's high, and it's the familiar situation the model was trained in.
  3. No. Any single frame looks confident, but the answer changes from frame to frame. The flicker is the real signal: the input sits on the border between two classes.

#Exercise 1: Predict the bars

A model's raw scores for one frame are Rock 3.0, Paper 3.0, Scissors 0.0, Nothing 0.0. Estimate the four percentages before you look.

Need a hint?

Equal scores get equal shares. A gap of 3 is big after softmax: each point of gap multiplies the share by about 2.7.

Show solution

Rock and Paper each get about 48%, and the other two about 2% each. In the preview this looks like a two-way tie, which is exactly what it is: the model sees a hand that fits Rock and Paper equally and is sure it's neither of the others.

#Exercise 2: Build a sorter and hold items out

  1. Before recording anything, split your items. For each class, put one or two items in a bag marked TEST. These are your unseen objects; they never go in front of the camera during recording.
  2. Start an image project with classes Recycling, Trash, and Nothing.
  3. Record about 60 samples per class using the remaining items. Hold each item at different angles, crushed and uncrushed if it's a can, on the table and in your hand. Nothing is the empty table, and your empty hand.
  4. Train with the defaults.
  5. Test each training item three times, then each TEST item three times. Write the top class and confidence each time.

Predict before testing: will the TEST items score lower, the same, or higher?

Need a hint?

The model has seen every angle of the training cans. Has it seen this label, this color, this shape?

Show solution

Expected result: training items come back right almost every time, usually above 95%. TEST items are less reliable. Something close in look to a training item (another aluminum can) often still works, at lower confidence. Something with a new look is where it fails: a glass jar when you trained on no glass, or a shiny chip bag that gets called Recycling because shiny and crinkly looked like a crushed can.

That's the model telling you what it actually learned: shine, color, and shape, not what the item is made of. Your log should report the TEST-item accuracy as the sorter's score, not the training-item one.

#Exercise 3: Change the surface

Test your TEST items again, this time on a different surface: the floor, a patterned cloth, or a colored sheet of paper instead of the table you trained on.

Need a hint?

In Module 2 you saw that a model learns whatever differs between classes, including backgrounds. What's the background in most of your sorter's samples?

Show solution

Expected result: accuracy drops again, and Nothing starts showing up for real items (or real items get pulled toward whichever class you held up most often near that color). Most of every sample is the table, so a new surface changes most of the picture. The fix is the same as in Module 2: record every class on two or three surfaces. Then retest on the TEST items, not the training ones.

#Exercise 4: Things with no class

Hold up things that are neither recycling nor trash: your phone, a shoe, a stuffed toy, your face. Write the bars for each.

Need a hint?

How many choices does the model have, and must it use one of them?

Show solution

Expected result: each one gets a confident answer, often 90% or more, in Recycling, Trash, or Nothing. A phone, with its glass and metal, frequently comes out as Recycling. The model must split 100% across three classes and has no "that's not waste" option.

Two practical fixes: make Nothing cover more ("not an item to sort": empty table, hands, phones, people passing), and, in an application, don't act on any reading you can't trust. The next exercise picks that line.

#Exercise 5: Choose a confidence threshold

A sorter could act only when the top class is at or above a threshold, and otherwise ask a person. Here are 30 unseen test results, each the top confidence and whether the answer was right. For thresholds of 50, 70, 80, 90, and 95, how many items would the sorter act on, how many of those would be wrong, and how many go to a person? Which threshold would you pick for a school cafeteria?

Need a hint?

For each threshold, count the values at or above it in each row. Items below the threshold aren't wrong; they're handed off.

Show solution

As the threshold rises, wrong actions fall, but more items go to a person. At 50% the sorter acts on everything and gets 9 wrong. At 90% it acts on 17 items with 2 wrong and hands off 13. At 95% only 1 of its 12 actions is wrong, but 18 of 30 items need a person, which defeats the point of a sorter.

For a cafeteria, 80% or 90% is a reasonable choice, and whichever you pick, you'd say so in your log: "acts at 90%; on our unseen test, 2 of its 17 actions were wrong, and it handed off 13 of 30 items." Notice that no threshold removes every error: one wrong answer was at 99%.

#Exercise 6: Write the sorter's test plan

Write an unseen test plan for your sorter that someone else could follow: which items, how many photos or tries per class, which surfaces and lighting, and who handles the items. Keep it to one screen.

Need a hint?

Reuse the structure of the rock, paper, scissors test plan: what changes in real use, at least 10 per class, truth written down first, and nothing from the test ever trained on.

Show solution

#Challenge: Fool it on purpose

Find something that makes your sorter say Recycling at 95% or more when no recyclable is there. Try a photo of a can shown on your phone screen, a drawing of a bottle, or a piece of foil crumpled into a ball.

Need a hint?

The Teachable Machine FAQ suggests exactly this: try tricking the model with a photo or a drawing of an object. Ask what the model can and can't sense through a webcam.

Show solution

Expected result: a photo of a can on a phone screen often scores very high for Recycling, because to a webcam it looks almost exactly like a can. Crumpled foil can pass as a crushed can too. Drawings are less reliable: a detailed color drawing may work; a stick-figure sketch usually doesn't.

The lesson for real use: an image model judges how things look from one angle, not what they're made of or whether they're real. A real sorter would need either more information (a scale, a metal sensor) or a person checking the cases where looks can lie. Write your fooling examples in your log; they're excellent unseen test items for the next version.

What you'll learn

  • Read a confusion matrix: rows are what each test item really was, columns are what the model said.
  • Name a false positive and a false negative for any class you choose.
  • Find the class pair a model confuses most, straight from the matrix.
  • Decide which error type costs more in a given app, and say why.

Two school clubs build recycling sorters with Teachable Machine. Each one points a webcam at an item and says Recycling or Trash. Both clubs test on the same 100 items, 50 of each kind, and both report the same score: 90 out of 100 right.

Same accuracy, but these are very different machines. Sorter A throws 10 clean cans and bottles into the trash. Sorter B sends 10 pieces of trash, like greasy pizza boxes and plastic bags, into the recycling. A recycling plant cares a lot about that difference, because a bale of paper with food waste in it can be rejected whole. One number hid the thing that mattered.

#Rows are the truth, columns are the guess

A confusion matrix is a table that counts every test result by two things: what the item really was, and what the model said. Teachable Machine draws one for you: in the Training panel, open Advanced, click Under the hood, then click Calculate confusion matrix. Its labels say Class down the side, for what the sample really is, and Prediction along the bottom, for what the model guessed. We'll use the same layout in this course.

You don't need to write the code below. It draws the two sorters' results so you can practice reading the picture.

Here's how to read it. The diagonal from top-left to bottom-right holds the right answers: Recycling called Recycling, Trash called Trash. Every cell off the diagonal is a mistake, and its position tells you exactly which mistake. Sorter A's 10 sits in the Recycling row, Trash column: real recyclables that the model called trash. Sorter B's 10 sits in the Trash row, Recycling column: real trash that the model let into recycling.

A quick habit: read a row left to right and say "Of the things that were really X, the model called this many A, this many B." Each row adds up to how many test items of that class you used.

#False positives and false negatives: pick a class first

Here's the intuition. A smoke alarm has one job: shout "fire!" when there's a fire. If it goes off because you burned some toast, that's a false positive: it said yes, and the answer was no. If it stays quiet during a real fire, that's a false negative: it said no, and the answer was yes.

Now precisely. Choose the class you care about and call it the "positive" class. Then:

Model says the class Model says something else
Item really is the class true positive false negative (missed it)
Item is something else false positive (false alarm) true negative

With Recycling as the class you care about, Sorter A makes 10 false negatives (recyclables it missed) and Sorter B makes 10 false positives (trash it wrongly accepted). Notice that the words flip if you pick Trash instead: Sorter B's mistakes become false negatives for Trash. That's why you always say which class you mean: "10 false positives for Recycling."

In matrix terms, for any class: its false negatives are the off-diagonal cells in its row, and its false positives are the off-diagonal cells in its column.

#Bigger matrices: find the cell that hurts most

Most models have more than two classes. Here are made-up results for a rock, paper, scissors model tested on 10 fresh tries of each sign, recorded on a different day from the training data.

Your eye goes straight to the 4 in the Scissors row, Paper column. Four out of ten Scissors tries were called Paper. Everything else is a 1 or 0. That one cell tells you what to fix, and it also tells you what not to touch: Paper itself is perfect on its own row, so the problem is that Paper is too eager to claim things.

The same counts, as false positives and false negatives per class:

Scissors has 4 false negatives and Paper has 4 false positives. It's the same four mistakes, counted from each side. When you see a matching pair like that, you've found two classes the model can't separate well, and your next job is to figure out why. The next lesson does exactly that with a real model.

#Which mistake costs more depends on the app

A model doesn't know what its mistakes cost. You do. Before you fix anything, decide which error you'd rather have, because some fixes trade one for the other.

App False positive looks like False negative looks like Usually worse
Smart doorbell sound detector Phone buzzes when the TV plays a ding A real visitor gets no answer False negative
Recycling sorter Trash contaminates the recycling A can goes to the landfill False positive
Posture reminder Nagged while sitting fine Slouches for an hour, no reminder Depends on the user
Sign-language letter helper Types a letter you didn't sign Ignores a letter you did sign False positive (wrong text is confusing)

The last column is a judgment, and reasonable people disagree. What matters is that you write it down before you look at the numbers, so you don't pick whichever story makes your model look good.

#Why Teachable Machine's own matrix often looks perfect

Teachable Machine holds back 15% of your samples as test samples and trains on the other 85%. Its confusion matrix and Calculate accuracy per class both use that 15%. The catch: webcam samples are recorded in bursts at many frames a second, so a test frame is often nearly identical to a training frame grabbed a split second earlier. The model has, in effect, seen the answer.

So treat the built-in matrix as a smoke test. If it shows mistakes, take them seriously. If it shows a perfect diagonal, that proves very little. The matrix you trust is the one you fill in yourself from unseen tries, like the 40 rock, paper, scissors tries above.

⚠️ Watch out

Reading the matrix sideways. If you read columns as the truth, you'll fix the wrong class. In the rock, paper, scissors example you'd conclude "Paper is being missed" and record more Paper, which makes Paper even greedier and the Scissors problem worse. Always check the axis labels first: in Teachable Machine, Class (the truth) runs down the side.

⚠️ Watch out

Fixing errors with test items. It's tempting to drag the four misread Scissors photos into the Scissors class and retrain. The next test on those same photos will look perfect, because the model has now studied them. Keep your unseen test set out of training forever, and collect new examples of the problem instead.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1In a doorbell model, the matrix shows 6 in the Doorbell row, Background Noise column. What happened?

  • The row is the truth (it was a doorbell) and the column is the guess (background noise), so the model missed six rings.

  • That would be in the Background Noise row, Doorbell column.

  • Correct answers sit on the diagonal, where row and column are the same class.

Show answer

A. The row is the truth (it was a doorbell) and the column is the guess (background noise), so the model missed six rings.

2Two sorters both score 90%. What extra information do you need to choose between them?

  • Equal accuracy can hide opposite kinds of mistakes, as Sorters A and B showed.

  • The matrix shows where the errors land; your app decides which errors you can live with.

  • Training settings don't tell you what kind of mistakes the model makes on real items.

Show answer

B. The matrix shows where the errors land; your app decides which errors you can live with.

3Scissors has 4 false negatives and Paper has 4 false positives, all in the same cell. What's the best first fix?

  • Paper is already over-claiming. More Paper data tends to make that worse.

  • Then the game can't recognize Scissors at all.

  • The error is specific, so the fix should be too. Find the pattern first, then add data that covers it.

Show answer

C. The error is specific, so the fix should be too. Find the pattern first, then add data that covers it.

4Teachable Machine's built-in confusion matrix shows a perfect diagonal. What should you conclude?

  • The built-in test samples come from the same recording bursts as the training samples, so they're very easy.

  • A perfect score on near-duplicate frames says little about new hands, rooms, or lighting.

Show answer

B. A perfect score on near-duplicate frames says little about new hands, rooms, or lighting.

Key takeaways

  • In a confusion matrix, each row is what items really were, each column is what the model said, and the diagonal is right answers.
  • A false positive is a false alarm for a class; a false negative is a miss. Always say which class you mean.
  • For any class: false negatives are the rest of its row, false positives are the rest of its column.
  • The biggest off-diagonal cell is where to start fixing, and a matching row and column usually means two classes look alike to the model.
  • Decide which mistake costs more for your app before you start changing data.

#Further reading

  • Thresholds and the confusion matrix (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course page, with an interactive example of how false positives and false negatives trade against each other.
  • Errors + Graceful Failure (opens in a new tab): Google's People + AI Guidebook chapter on how real products plan for the mistakes their models will make.
  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): the "Why isn't it working like I want it to?" section suggests deliberately confusing your model to learn where it breaks.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run an unseen test and record every result on a test sheet.
  • Turn the sheet into a confusion matrix and pick the one error worth fixing first.
  • Trace that error to a specific gap in the training data.
  • Make one targeted data change, retrain, retest on the same photos, and log the result honestly.

Your rock, paper, scissors model from earlier modules probably works well when you sit where you trained it. This build finds out where it doesn't, and fixes the worst case without breaking anything else. Here's the finished product, a log entry comparing two versions on the same 40 photos:

The numbers in this lesson are an example. Yours will differ, and that's the point: you'll make the same kind of entry from your own model.

#Step 1: Run the unseen test and fill in a test sheet

You need test photos the model has never seen. Use the unseen test set from Module 4. If you don't have one, make it now: with your computer's camera app (not Teachable Machine), take 10 photos of each sign in a room or light you didn't train in, and name them r01.jpg to r10.jpg, p01.jpg and so on. Put them in a folder called test-set. Those 40 photos never go into a class. Ever.

Then open your saved project (☰ › Open project from file), click Train Model, and in the Preview panel switch the input dropdown from Webcam to File. Drop in each photo and write down what the model says:

The "what I notice" column is the most important part of the sheet. Write it while the photo is in front of you, before you've decided what the problem is.

#Step 2: Draw the matrix

Type your counts into the grid below and run it. The code is the same drawing helper as in the last lesson; you only edit the numbers.

Read the off-diagonal cells from biggest to smallest. The 4 in the Scissors row, Paper column is four times larger than anything else. The two 1s between Rock and Nothing are small enough to be bad luck on 10 photos; if they show up again next test, they'll get their own fix.

#Step 3: Find what the mistakes have in common

Now go back to the four Scissors photos the model called Paper and read your notes column. All four say fingers spread wide. That's your pattern: a wide V.

A pattern in the test photos is only half the story. The other half is in the training data. Open the Scissors class and scroll through its thumbnails. In this example, nearly every Scissors sample shows a narrow V, with the two fingers close together. The model was never shown a wide V labeled Scissors. What it had seen with spread fingers was Paper, so that's what it guessed.

Write the cause down as one sentence you could prove wrong: "Wide-V Scissors look like Paper because training Scissors only had narrow V's." If the fix doesn't help, that sentence was wrong, and you've still learned something.

#Step 4: Make one targeted change

The fix follows directly from the cause: show the model wide-V Scissors, labeled Scissors.

  1. Open the Scissors class and click Webcam.
  2. Record about 30 new samples of a wide V: right hand and left hand, close and far, facing the camera and slightly turned. Short bursts, moving your hand between them, like in Module 2.
  3. Now look at the class count. It jumped from about 98 to 128, while the other classes sit near 95. Module 3 showed what an oversized class does: it starts winning arguments it shouldn't. So delete 30 of the old narrow-V samples, picking ones that look almost identical to their neighbors.

You've replaced 30 samples instead of piling on, which keeps the classes balanced, and you changed only one thing. Don't also tweak epochs, re-record Rock, or rename classes in the same round. If several things change at once and the results move, you can't tell which change did it.

⚠️ Watch out

Don't drag s03.jpg, s05.jpg, s08.jpg, or s09.jpg into the Scissors class, even though they're exactly the examples the model needs. Once they're in training, your next test on them measures memory, not skill. Record new wide-V samples instead, and keep the test folder untouched.

#Step 5: Retrain and retest on the same 40 photos

Click Train Model with the same Advanced settings as v1. Then repeat Step 1 exactly: same 40 photos, same order, same way of reading the top prediction. Using the same photos is what makes the comparison fair. New photos would change two things at once, the model and the test.

Put the v2 counts next to the v1 counts:

Then let Python list exactly which cells moved, so you don't miss a small change:

The cell you targeted dropped from 4 to 1. The hypothesis held up. But a new mistake appeared: one Paper photo is now called Scissors. Look at it. In this example, it's a Paper photo taken side-on, where three fingers hide behind the other two and the hand looks like a wide V. That's a genuinely borderline photo, and it's the price of teaching the model that spread fingers aren't automatically Paper.

#Step 6: Decide, save, and log

Compare honestly. The big error shrank by three, a new small one appeared, and the total went from 34 to 36. That's a clear win, so keep v2. If the new error had been large, or in the class you care most about, you'd weigh it differently.

  1. Open ☰ › Download project as file and name it rock-paper-scissors-v2- plus today's date.
  2. Add the change log entry from the top of this lesson to your project log, with your own numbers.
  3. Leave the test-set folder exactly as it is. You'll use it again for every future version.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why retest v2 on the same 40 photos instead of taking fresh ones?

  • With the same photos, any difference in the matrix comes from your data change, not from an easier or harder test.

  • You can upload the same file as often as you like; this is about fair comparison.

  • Preview never adds anything to your classes.

Show answer

A. With the same photos, any difference in the matrix comes from your data change, not from an easier or harder test.

2Why delete 30 old Scissors samples after recording 30 new ones?

  • There's no such limit. The reason is balance.

  • An oversized class tends to win close calls, which would trade one error for another.

  • Every sample is used again each time you train.

Show answer

B. An oversized class tends to win close calls, which would trade one error for another.

3v2 fixed Scissors → Paper but added one Paper → Scissors error. What's the most reasonable conclusion?

  • The targeted error dropped from 4 to 1 and the total rose from 34 to 36. That's an improvement with a small side effect.

  • One new mistake on 10 photos might be a borderline photo. Logging it means you'll notice if it grows.

  • That puts a test photo into training, which makes the next test meaningless.

Show answer

B. One new mistake on 10 photos might be a borderline photo. Logging it means you'll notice if it grows.

Key takeaways

  • A test sheet with a "what I notice" column is what turns a matrix into a diagnosis.
  • Fix the biggest off-diagonal cell first; leave single stray errors until they repeat.
  • Find the cause in two places: what the misread test photos share, and what the training class is missing.
  • Change one thing per version, replace samples to keep balance, and never train on test photos.
  • Retest on the same unseen photos, compare cell by cell, and log the trade-off you accepted.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Fix the Rock → Nothing error as a separate version (v3). Do the dark photos have something in common, and does your Rock class have any dark samples?
  • With their permission, have a friend do 10 tries of each sign. Does your v2 still hold up on hands it has never seen?
  • Compare the built-in Calculate confusion matrix result for v1 and v2. Did it notice the Scissors problem at all?

#Further reading

  • Dividing the original dataset (opens in a new tab): Google's Machine Learning Crash Course on why a test set must stay separate from training, including the problem of near-duplicate examples.
  • Data Collection + Evaluation (opens in a new tab): the People + AI Guidebook chapter on planning data so it matches the situations your model will meet.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Count false positives and false negatives for a chosen class from any confusion matrix.
  • Name the confused class pair and the direction of the confusion.
  • Match an error pattern to a likely gap in the training data, and propose a targeted fix.
  • Judge a before-and-after comparison by the error that matters, not only by accuracy.

#Warm-up

A smoke alarm was tested 20 times with smoke and 20 times without. With smoke it went off 19 times. Without smoke it went off 3 times. How many false positives and false negatives for Smoke?

Show solution

3 false positives (it went off with no smoke) and 1 false negative (it stayed quiet once when there was smoke). Write the matrix if it helps: the Smoke row is 19 and 1, the No smoke row is 3 and 17.

#Exercise 1: Count errors for one class

A smart doorbell sound detector has three classes. Here's its test on 60 one-second clips:

How many false negatives and false positives does Doorbell have? What does each one mean for the person at the door?

Sample answer format: Doorbell: ? false negatives, ? false positives

Need a hint?

False negatives are the off-diagonal cells in the Doorbell row. False positives are the off-diagonal cells in the Doorbell column.

Show solution

Four real rings were missed: three were heard as background noise and one as a knock. Those four visitors stand outside with no notification. The two false positives are background sounds that buzzed your phone for nothing, which is annoying but harmless.

#Exercise 2: Which letters does the sign helper mix up?

A sign-language letter helper recognizes the fingerspelled letters A, S, and B, plus Nothing. It was tested on 10 unseen tries per class:

Name the confused pair, say which direction is worse, and suggest why these two letters in particular get confused.

Need a hint?

Look for errors that appear in both directions between the same two classes. Then think about how the two handshapes actually differ.

Show solution

A and S are confused both ways: A called S three times, S called A twice. Confusion in both directions usually means the two classes look nearly the same to the model. Both letters are a closed fist; the difference is mostly where the thumb sits (alongside the fist for A, across the front of the fingers for S). That's a small detail in a webcam frame. A targeted fix: record new A and S samples close to the camera with the thumb clearly visible, from a few angles, in both classes. B and Nothing are perfect, so leave them alone.

#Exercise 3: Match the symptom to the cause

For each symptom, pick the most likely data gap and a targeted fix.

  1. A posture reminder (a pose project with Upright and Slouching) calls you Upright whenever you sit on the left side of the camera view, even while slouching.
  2. The doorbell detector misses rings, but only while the dishwasher is running.
  3. A recycling sorter calls every crumpled item Trash, including crumpled clean paper.
Need a hint?

For each one, ask: what condition is present in the failing tests that was missing from the training samples of the class that lost?

Show solution
  1. Position in the frame. Teachable Machine's pose model tracks where your body is in the frame, not only its shape, so the FAQ warns that standing on the left looks like a different pose from standing on the right. Training was probably all centered. Fix: record both Upright and Slouching at left, center, and right positions.
  2. Missing background condition. No Doorbell samples were recorded with the dishwasher running, so the dishwasher sound drowns out what the model learned. Fix: record new Doorbell clips with the dishwasher on, and add dishwasher noise to Background Noise too, so the model learns that dishwasher alone means "nothing".
  3. Recycling had only flat paper. The model learned "crumpled means trash". Fix: add crumpled clean paper to Recycling, and keep the class sizes even.

#Exercise 4: Which error would you reduce?

For each app, say which error type you'd reduce first, and what you'd accept in exchange.

  1. A game where a pose triggers "jump".
  2. A helper that warns a cyclist when it hears a car horn behind them.
  3. A sorter that sends anything it isn't sure about to a human checker.
Need a hint?

Picture each mistake happening for real. Which one makes the person stop trusting the app, or puts them at risk?

Show solution
  1. False positives. A character jumping when you didn't ask feels broken. You'd accept a few missed jumps, which players read as "I didn't do it right".
  2. False negatives. Missing a real horn could hurt someone. You'd accept extra false alarms, as long as they aren't so frequent that the cyclist starts ignoring them.
  3. Here the human checker changes the trade-off: an "unsure" item costs a few seconds of someone's time. You'd reduce wrong confident answers in both directions and accept more items going to the checker.

#Exercise 5: Did the fix really help?

A school's recycling sorter was retrained after someone added more Recycling examples. The plant that takes the recycling says trash in the recycling (a false positive for Recycling) is the costly error. Same 100 test items both times:

Compute accuracy and Recycling's false positives for both versions. Is the new version better for this plant?

Need a hint?

Accuracy is the diagonal over the total. The false positives for Recycling are in the Trash row, Recycling column.

Show solution

Accuracy went up from 91% to 94%, but false positives went up from 3 to 5. Adding Recycling examples made the model more eager to say Recycling, which fixed misses and created more of the costly mistake. For this plant it's not a clear improvement. A better next step is a targeted look at the five trash items that got through: what do they share?

#Exercise 6: Catch the cheating retest

A classmate's log says:

What's wrong with this conclusion, and how could they get a fair answer now?

Need a hint?

What has v2 seen that v1 hadn't, and is the test still "unseen" for v2?

Show solution

The 9 hardest test photos are now training data, so v2 has studied the answers. A perfect score on photos it trained on says nothing about new photos. The fix: take a new set of 40 unseen photos (different from both training and the old test), run both v1 and v2 on it, and compare those results. The 9 photos can stay in training, but the old test set can't be used as a test for v2 any more.

#Challenge: A full repair round on your own model

Run one complete repair round on your rock, paper, scissors model or any other Teachable Machine model you've built: unseen test sheet with notes, matrix, one hypothesis written as a sentence, one data change, retrain, retest on the same items, and a log entry. Use this template to draw your before and after matrices and list every cell that moved. Change the labels and counts to yours.

Your log entry should end with a decision (keep or roll back) and one sentence on the trade-off you accepted.

What you'll learn

  • Choose between Upload (shareable link) and Download, and between the Tensorflow.js, Tensorflow, and Tensorflow Lite tabs.
  • Explain what leaves your computer at each step, and who can use a shared model.
  • Spot what a model reveals through its labels and its behavior, even though your samples stay private.
  • List the parts of a model card and say why a model file can't replace one.

Here is everything a real, public Teachable Machine model says about itself. It's the example model used in the ml5.js documentation, and anyone can fetch this file from its link:

You learn two labels, a date, and some version numbers. You don't learn who trained it, on what pictures, whether it works at dusk, or what it should never be used for. If you built an app on this model and it failed at sunset, the file couldn't have warned you. Exporting is three clicks; exporting responsibly means sending the missing information along with the model.

#Three tabs, two destinations

When your model is trained, the Export Model button sits at the top of the Preview panel. It opens a window titled "Export your model to use it in projects," with three tabs. The tabs decide what kind of file you get; the choice inside the first tab decides where it lives.

Tab and option What you get Where it runs
Tensorflow.js, Upload (shareable link) A link to your model, hosted by Teachable Machine, plus ready-made code snippets Any web page or p5.js sketch
Tensorflow.js, Download A zip with model.json, weights.bin, and metadata.json Your own website or app, from your own files
Tensorflow (Keras or Savedmodel) A model for Python programs, plus a labels.txt Python on a computer
Tensorflow Lite (Floating point, Quantized, or EdgeTPU) A small model file for devices, plus a labels.txt Phones, Raspberry Pi, Coral boards

Not every project gets every tab. Image projects have all three. Audio projects offer Tensorflow.js and Tensorflow Lite. Pose projects export as Tensorflow.js only. (Google has since renamed TensorFlow Lite to LiteRT, so newer guides may use that name.)

For this course you'll mostly use Tensorflow.js, because it runs in a browser, which is where Module 7's apps live.

#What leaves your computer, step by step

Teachable Machine is careful about your samples. Recording and training happen inside your browser tab. According to its FAQ, your samples aren't sent to any server unless you save the project to your own Google Drive.

Exporting is where things leave. The diagram follows each path:

Three facts from the FAQ and the export window are worth knowing exactly:

  • Upload sends the model, not the examples. The FAQ calls the model "the mathematical program that predicts which class you're showing it." Your photos and recordings stay with you.
  • Anyone with the link can use it. They can't change your model, but they can load it into their own projects. And if your web page loads the model, anyone who views your page's code can find the link.
  • Some conversions send a few samples. The Tensorflow Lite Quantized and EdgeTPU options upload a subset of your data to do the conversion. The export window says it isn't stored on the server, but it does leave your computer.

A shared link is unlisted, not private. Treat an uploaded model as public: once someone has copied the link or downloaded the files, you can't pull those copies back.

#What a model reveals without its samples

"My photos weren't uploaded" doesn't mean nothing about you or your participants was shared. A model gives away information in two ways.

Its labels. Class names travel with the model. Here's a downloaded metadata.json from a model a student made to "check who's at the door":

Three people's names are now attached to a tool that claims to recognize them. Nobody had to see a single photo.

Its behavior. Anyone can show the model new pictures and watch the scores. A model trained on your classmates' faces, shared publicly, is a working tool for picking those classmates out of other photos. A voice model can be probed to find out whose voice a clip sounds like. Researchers have also shown that, in some cases, trained models can leak details of the examples they learned from. The samples stayed home; what the model learned from them didn't.

#Consent covers the use, not only the recording

When a friend agreed to be recorded for your rock, paper, scissors project, they agreed to that: hand photos, in your browser, for a course project. Uploading a model trained on their face or voice is a different use, with a different audience. Ask again, and tell them exactly what will be shared and where.

A simple rule for this course: models that recognize particular people (faces, voices, names) stay on your computer. Models that recognize things or gestures can be shared once every person in the data has said yes to sharing.

#A model card is the label on the box

A model card is a short document that travels with a model and tells a stranger what it's for and how far to trust it. The idea comes from a 2019 paper by researchers at Google, "Model Cards for Model Reporting," and it's now common on sites that host models. A card for a Teachable Machine project fits on one page:

Section What to write
What it does One sentence: input, output, purpose
Classes The exact labels, and what each one means in camera terms
Data How many samples per class, who appears, where and how they were recorded, and that everyone agreed
How it was tested Your unseen test: how many items, and the confusion matrix results
Works well when Lighting, distance, background, people similar to the data
Known weak spots The errors you found, in plain words
Don't use it for Uses it was never tested for, or that could hurt someone
Version, date, contact So people know which model they have and who to tell about problems

Compare that table with the metadata.json at the top of this lesson. The file covers part of one row (the labels) and a date. Everything else exists only if you write it.

⚠️ Watch out

Personal names as class labels. A class called Maya publishes Maya's name with every copy of the model. Use labels that describe what the camera sees (Person 1, Thumbs up, Doorbell), and keep any key that maps them to real people off the internet.

⚠️ Watch out

"I downloaded it, so it's private." A downloaded zip is private only until you put it somewhere public. If your website loads model.json from a public folder (GitHub Pages, for example), anyone can download all three files, labels included. The privacy decision happens when you publish the files, not when you click Download.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You click Upload my model. What is now on Google's servers?

  • The FAQ says the examples are not published with the model.

  • The upload is the model only. The link works for anyone who has it, and they can't change the model.

  • The model is uploaded when you click the button; sharing the link only decides who knows where it is.

Show answer

B. The upload is the model only. The link works for anyone who has it, and they can't change the model.

2A pose model for a dance game needs to run on a website. Which export do you choose?

  • Pose projects export as Tensorflow.js, which is the format browsers run.

  • Pose projects don't offer Tensorflow Lite, and it's meant for phones and small devices anyway.

  • Keras is for Python programs, and pose projects don't offer it.

Show answer

A. Pose projects export as Tensorflow.js, which is the format browsers run.

3Your model recognizes three friends' faces. All three agreed to be recorded for a class project. What should happen before you upload it?

  • They agreed to a recording for a class project, not to a public tool that can recognize them.

  • Renaming hides their names, but the model still recognizes their faces for anyone with the link.

  • Sharing turns it into a tool that can pick them out of other photos, which is a much bigger use than they agreed to.

Show answer

C. Sharing turns it into a tool that can pick them out of other photos, which is a much bigger use than they agreed to.

4Which information is in the exported model files, and which do you have to write in a model card yourself?

  • The metadata has labels, a timestamp, and versions. It has nothing about data, testing, or limits.

  • That's exactly the gap a model card fills.

Show answer

B. That's exactly the gap a model card fills.

Key takeaways

  • Export Model has three tabs: Tensorflow.js for browsers, Tensorflow for Python, and Tensorflow Lite for phones and small devices.
  • Upload (shareable link) puts the model, not your samples, on Google's servers; anyone with the link can use it.
  • A model reveals information through its labels and its behavior, even when no sample leaves your computer.
  • Consent to be recorded isn't consent to be recognized by a public model. Keep people-recognizing models private.
  • A model card tells people what the model does, what data and tests stand behind it, and where it fails. The files can't say any of that.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): the "Saving & Exporting" section answers who can access your samples and who can use a published model, in the team's own words.
  • Google Model Cards (opens in a new tab): short, readable examples of real model cards for face detection and object detection models.
  • Model Cards for Model Reporting (opens in a new tab): the original 2019 paper. The first two pages explain the idea clearly, even if the rest is technical.

What you'll learn

  • Check labels, consent, and version before anything leaves your computer.
  • Upload a model with Upload my model and see the link the way a stranger sees it.
  • Download the Tensorflow.js files and read what metadata.json contains.
  • Write a model card whose test numbers come from your unseen test, then check it with a reader.

By the end of this build you'll have a small release folder for your model. Anyone you hand it to can use the model and know when to trust it:

#Step 1: Check before you export

Open rock-paper-scissors-v2 from Module 5 (☰ › Open project from file) and go through this list. Every "no" stops the export until you fix it.

The consent line is the one people skip. If a friend's hands are in your Scissors class, ask them now: "I'm putting a model trained on these online, at a link anyone could use. Is that OK?" If they say no, remove their samples, retrain, and retest before going on.

#Step 2: Upload and copy the link

  1. Click Export Model at the top of the Preview panel.
  2. Stay on the Tensorflow.js tab and choose Upload (shareable link).
  3. Click Upload my model. The button reads Uploading... for a few seconds.
  4. When it finishes, the window shows Your sharable link: with a URL like https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/models/AbC123xYz/. Click Copy.

Make model-link.txt and paste the link in with its version:

Below the link, the export window also shows code snippets for Javascript and p5.js. You'll use those in Module 7, and you can always come back here for them.

#Step 3: Open the link as a stranger would

Open a private (incognito) browser window and paste your link. A private window isn't signed in and has no history, so you see the page exactly as someone who just received the link does.

The page explains what the link is, lists the files it hosts, and offers to preview the model live, along with a way to report the model. Click the live preview and try a few signs. Two things to notice:

  • Your class names are public. They're part of the model, so they show up for anyone. That's why Step 1 checked them.
  • There's no explanation of how well it works, or where it fails. The page can't know. That's the model card's job.

#Step 4: Download a backup and look inside

Back in the export window, switch to Download and click Download my model. You get tm-my-image-model.zip. Unzip it into your release folder and you'll find three files: model.json (the model's structure), weights.bin (the numbers it learned), and metadata.json. Open metadata.json in any text editor. It looks something like this, with your own date and versions:

The labels are in the same order as your classes. The download is your backup: if you ever lose the project file, these three files still run the model.

#Step 5: Let the test sheet fill in the numbers

The most important section of a model card, "How it was tested," should be copied from your unseen test, not typed from memory or taken from Accuracy per class (which uses the easy built-in test samples, as Module 5 showed). Paste your v2 counts below and the cell writes that section for you:

The output is plain Markdown you can paste into the card. Because it reads the labels in the same order as the model, the rows can't get shuffled by accident.

#Step 6: Write the rest of the card

The other sections come from your project log and your own judgment. Here's a finished card for the example model. Write yours in a file called MODEL_CARD.md, or in a document next to your project:

Look at the "Known weak spots" line: every item came from a real test result or a real gap in the data. A card that says "works great!" with no weak spots isn't humble, it's untested.

#Step 7: Run the reader test

Give the link and the card to someone who hasn't seen your project, and ask them three questions using only the card:

  1. Would this work in a dark room?
  2. Could I use it to check who is at the door?
  3. Which version is this, and when was it made?

If they can't answer one, the card is missing something. Fix it now, because in a month you'll be the stranger too.

💡 Tip

When you retrain later, the export window's button changes to Update my cloud model so you can push the new version to your link. Every app using that link gets the new model, so update the card's version, test results, and date at the same time.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why open your link in a private browser window?

  • A private window is the closest you can get to being a stranger to your own model.

  • It works in any window; private just removes your own context.

  • The model is already on Google's servers once you've uploaded it.

Show answer

A. A private window is the closest you can get to being a stranger to your own model.

2Where should the card's "How it was tested" numbers come from?

  • Those use the built-in test samples, which are near-copies of training frames and tend to look too good.

  • That test used photos the model never saw, in different conditions, which is what a reader needs to know.

  • A guess can't be checked, and it tends to be optimistic.

Show answer

B. That test used photos the model never saw, in different conditions, which is what a reader needs to know.

3A friend whose hands are in your data says no to sharing. What do you do?

  • Consent is their decision, not yours.

  • Removing samples changes the model, so it needs a new test before the card can describe it.

  • A download can still be shared later, and it's still a model trained on their hands.

Show answer

B. Removing samples changes the model, so it needs a new test before the card can describe it.

Key takeaways

  • Check labels, sharing consent, and version before exporting; consent to record isn't consent to share.
  • Upload my model gives a public link; view it in a private window to see what strangers see.
  • Keep the downloaded zip as a backup: model.json, weights.bin, and metadata.json run the model on their own.
  • A model card's test numbers should come straight from your unseen test, and its weak spots from real results.
  • The reader test shows whether the card answers the questions a stranger will actually ask.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Put your card and link on a free GitHub Pages site or a shared class document, so the card is always next to the link.
  • When you make v3, write only what changed in the card, then compare the two cards side by side. Does the "Known weak spots" list get shorter?
  • Ask a classmate to try your model on their own hands, with the card in front of them. Add whatever they discover to the card.

#Further reading

  • Model Cards on Hugging Face (opens in a new tab): how the biggest model-sharing site asks people to document models, with sections that match the ones in this lesson.
  • Google Model Cards (opens in a new tab): finished cards from Google for real models; compare their "limitations" sections with yours.

What you'll learn

  • Match a project to the right export tab and option.
  • Find personal information in class labels and metadata, and rewrite it.
  • Spot the missing sections in a weak model card, and write limits from real test results.
  • Decide whether a model can be shared, based on who is in the data and what it recognizes.

#Warm-up

Without looking back: which export tab would you use for a model that runs in a web page, and which for a model that runs on an Android phone?

Show solution

Web page: Tensorflow.js (Upload for a link, or Download to host the files yourself). Android phone: Tensorflow Lite, the format built for phones and small devices.

#Exercise 1: Pick the export

Choose a tab and option for each project. One sentence of reasoning each.

  1. A p5.js sketch your class will open in the p5.js Web Editor.
  2. A museum kiosk with no internet connection, running a web page from its own hard drive.
  3. A Python program on a Raspberry Pi that sorts objects with a servo.
  4. A pose-controlled game on a website.
Need a hint?

Ask two questions each time: what runs the model (a browser, Python, or a small device), and does it have internet access to reach a hosted link?

Show solution
  1. Tensorflow.js, Upload (shareable link). The sketch can load the model straight from the link.
  2. Tensorflow.js, Download. The kiosk can't reach a link, so the three files (model.json, weights.bin, metadata.json) go on its drive next to the web page.
  3. Tensorflow Lite (Floating point is the simplest start), or Tensorflow (Keras) if the Pi runs full TensorFlow. Tensorflow Lite is built for small devices like the Pi.
  4. Tensorflow.js. It's the only option for pose projects, and it's the one browsers run anyway.

#Exercise 2: Audit the labels

A student is about to upload a household sound and image model with these class names. Which ones are a problem, and what would you rename them to?

Need a hint?

Labels travel with the model to everyone who has the link. Look for names, places that identify where someone lives or studies, and labels that tell a stranger nothing.

Show solution
  • Dad snoring: reveals a family member and something private about him. Rename to Snoring, or ask whether this class should be in a shared model at all.
  • Jake: a person's name in a model that recognizes him. Don't share a model that recognizes a particular person; keep this one private.
  • Room 214 door: points to a real place. Rename to Door.
  • Class 3: not private, just unhelpful. A stranger can't tell what it means. Rename it to what it detects, or delete it if it's a leftover.
  • Background Noise and Thumbs up are fine.

#Exercise 3: What does this file give away?

Someone posted a sound model link online. You fetch its metadata.json (audio models use wordLabels instead of labels):

List what a stranger now knows, and what they could do with the model itself.

Need a hint?

Think about the labels, the date, and then what happens if someone plays recordings into this model.

Show solution

From the file: the model recognizes two specific older people by voice and a dog, and it was made on 2 October 2026 at 21:43 UTC. From the model: anyone can play clips into it and see whether a voice scores as "Grandma" or "Grandpa", which makes it a rough tool for identifying those two people. The fix is to not share it; a voice model of particular people should stay on the computer that made it.

#Exercise 4: Fix a weak model card

Here's a whole model card from a classmate. Which sections from the Module 6 table are missing?

Need a hint?

Go through the table: what it does, classes, data, how it was tested, works well when, weak spots, don't use it for, version and date, contact.

Show solution

It has a vague purpose, the class names, and a version number. Missing:

  • Classes explained in camera terms (what counts as Recycling here?).
  • Data: how many samples, what items, where and how they were recorded.
  • How it was tested: no unseen test and no numbers. "Works really well" can't be checked.
  • Works well when and Known weak spots.
  • Don't use it for (for example: sorting for a real recycling plant without a human check).
  • Date and contact.

#Exercise 5: Write weak spots from real results

Your doorbell detector's unseen test sheet has these notes on its mistakes. Write the "Known weak spots" and "Don't use it for" sections.

Need a hint?

Turn each pattern into a plain sentence a user would understand. Then think about who might rely on this app and when a miss would really matter.

Show solution

Every line points back to a real result, and the "untested" line is as important as the failures.

#Exercise 6: Can this model be shared?

Use the flowchart to decide for each model, and say what has to happen first if the answer is "not yet".

  1. A thumbs-up and thumbs-down model trained only on your own hands.
  2. A sign helper trained on five club members' hands; four agreed to sharing, one hasn't answered.
  3. A classroom attendance model that recognizes each student's face; every student said yes.
  4. A dog-bark detector trained on your dog and a neighbor's dog, with the neighbor's permission.
Need a hint?

The first question in the flowchart is about what the model does, not about who agreed.

Show solution
  1. Share, after checking the labels and writing a card.
  2. Not yet. Silence isn't agreement. Remove the fifth member's samples (or wait for a clear yes), retrain, retest, then share.
  3. Keep it private. Even with everyone's agreement, a public face-recognition model can pick these students out of any photo, forever. Agreement to an attendance tool isn't agreement to that.
  4. Share: it recognizes dogs barking, not people, and the neighbor agreed. Write in the card that it was trained on two dogs only.

#Challenge: Release v3 with a changed card

You've retrained your rock, paper, scissors model as v3, adding dark-room Rock samples. The new unseen test gives Rock 10/10 and Nothing 10/10, with Paper and Scissors unchanged. Write the changes to the v2 card from Module 6 as a diff: lines starting with - are removed, lines with + are added.

Show solution

The version, the totals, the per-class lines, the weak spots, and the change itself all move together. Then click Update my cloud model so the link serves v3, and test the link in a private window again.
