What you'll learn

  • Describe the loop every model-powered app runs: camera, model, label, action.
  • Find the load, loop, and predict parts of Teachable Machine's exported JavaScript.
  • Pick the top class from a list of scores, by name rather than by position.
  • Use a confidence threshold, a hold time, and a cooldown so an app acts once per real gesture.

Picture a snake game you steer by pointing your hand up, down, left, or right at the webcam. You switch from Up to Left, and in the half second it takes your hand to move, the model's top label goes Up, Left, Up, Left, Up, Left. A game that obeys every frame makes the snake zigzag five times. You only asked for one turn.

The model isn't broken. Halfway through a movement, your hand really does look a bit like both signs. The fix lives in the app, in a few lines between "the model said" and "the game does". That's what this lesson is about.

#Every app runs the same loop

A Teachable Machine model never runs once. The app grabs a camera frame, hands it to the model, gets back a score for each class, decides what to do, and starts again, many times a second.

The boxes on the left are what Teachable Machine gives you. The diamond is what you write. Most beginner apps skip the diamond and wire the label straight to the action, which is exactly how you get a zigzagging snake.

#The code Teachable Machine gives you

After you upload a model (Module 6), the export window shows code snippets. This is its Javascript snippet for an image model, with a few comments trimmed. In the export window, your own link appears where this shows {{URL}}:

You don't need to understand every line. Find three parts:

  • Load. tmImage.load(modelURL, metadataURL) downloads model.json and metadata.json from your link. This is why the link matters: it's the only line that ties the page to your model.
  • Loop. requestAnimationFrame(loop) asks the browser to run loop again before the next screen refresh, so the page predicts as often as it can, up to about 60 times a second.
  • Predict. model.predict(webcam.canvas) returns one entry per class, each with a className and a probability from 0 to 1.

This code can't run inside this lesson page, because it needs your camera and your model's link. When you run it on a real web page, you'll see a Start button; click it, allow the camera, and a small webcam square appears with one line per class underneath, like Rock: 0.97, the numbers changing as you move. The next lesson runs a version of this in the p5.js Web Editor.

#A prediction is a list of scores

Each frame, predict() hands back a list like the one below. Your app's first job is to pick the winner. This part does run here, with a pretend frame:

The loop keeps whichever entry has the highest probability. The scores always add up to 1, because the model must split its belief across your classes. That's also why it never says "none of these": if you show it a banana, some class still wins. A Nothing or Background Noise class gives it an honest place to put that belief.

Notice that the app checks top.className, the label's name. It never assumes "Left is entry number 2".

#Three rules that calm a jumpy model

Here's a recording of 20 frames, about two-thirds of a second, while a player switches from Up to Left. Watch what a game does if it obeys every frame, compared with one that uses two rules: act only when confidence is at least 0.85, and only after the same label has won 4 frames in a row.

The naive app turned nine times for one real change. The steady app turned once, at frame 13. Read the frames again and you'll see why: the low-confidence frames during the switch never count, and the stray Right at frame 14 is far too unsure to matter.

Each rule has a job and a cost:

Rule What it stops What it costs
Threshold (act only above, say, 0.85) Half-formed gestures and "not sure" frames Misses gestures the model is only fairly sure of (more false negatives)
Hold (same label for several frames, or a few hundred milliseconds) Single-frame flickers A short delay before every action
Cooldown or re-arm (after acting, wait a few seconds, or wait for Nothing) The same gesture firing again and again You can't repeat an action quickly

These are the false positive and false negative trade-offs from Module 5, now under your control. A higher threshold means fewer false alarms and more misses.

Try it live below. Nothing here uses a camera: the page invents model output with as much flicker as you choose. Raise the jitter and watch the naive count run away while the steady app keeps up with the real changes. Then set the hold to 0 and see how much of the work the threshold alone does.

#Sounds and poses use the same loop, with two twists

Audio models listen instead of looking. The exported code calls recognizer.listen() with a function that runs each time a new one-second window of sound has been scored, and an options object:

Two of those options are rules you already know. probabilityThreshold is a built-in threshold: the function only runs when the top score beats it. overlapFactor sets how often the model checks: at 0.5, it scores the last second of audio every half second. Class names come from recognizer.wordLabels(), and the first class is always Background Noise.

Pose models take two steps per frame: model.estimatePose() finds your body's keypoints (shoulders, elbows, wrists, and so on), then model.predict() classifies those points. The twist is that the pose model also cares where you are in the frame, so an app that works when you sit in the middle may fail when you sit to one side.

#What you could build

Idea Project type The rule between label and action
Sign-language letter helper Image Type a letter when it's held at 0.9 or more for one second; then wait for Nothing before accepting the next letter
Smart doorbell sound detector Audio Notify when Doorbell scores 0.9 or more; then ignore doorbells for 10 seconds
Posture reminder Pose Play a gentle sound after Slouching has won for 10 seconds straight; reset the timer whenever Upright wins

Every row has a threshold, a hold, and a cooldown or re-arm. The numbers differ because the costs of mistakes differ.

⚠️ Watch out

Checking classes by position. Code like if (prediction[2].probability > 0.9) silently breaks if you ever add, delete, or reorder a class: entry 2 is now a different class, and nothing tells you. Always find the class by its name, as in prediction.find(p => p.className === "Left").

⚠️ Watch out

Left and right swap. Teachable Machine's training webcam is mirrored, like a selfie camera, which is why the snippet sets flip = true. If your app's camera isn't flipped the same way, a hand pointing left looks like a hand pointing right, and your snake turns the wrong way every time. Keep the flip setting the same as in training.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Your gesture app plays a sound effect about 60 times a second while you hold a thumbs-up. Which rule is missing?

  • A clear thumbs-up passes any sensible threshold, so the sound would still repeat.

  • Without one, every frame that shows a confident thumbs-up triggers the action again.

  • It helps when no hand is showing, but the problem here happens while your hand is showing.

Show answer

B. Without one, every frame that shows a confident thumbs-up triggers the action again.

2You raise the threshold from 0.7 to 0.95. What happens to errors?

  • The app ignores more uncertain frames, so it fires wrongly less often but also misses more real gestures.

  • A threshold trades one error for the other; it doesn't remove both.

  • That's what lowering the threshold does.

Show answer

A. The app ignores more uncertain frames, so it fires wrongly less often but also misses more real gestures.

3Which line ties the exported page to your own model?

  • That keeps the loop running; it would run with any model.

  • Swap the link and the same page runs a completely different model.

  • That sets up the camera, not the model.

Show answer

B. Swap the link and the same page runs a completely different model.

4Why does the model still name a class when you show it something it was never trained on?

  • It's how classifiers work, not a bug.

  • The model splits its belief across the classes it knows. A Nothing or Background Noise class gives it somewhere sensible to put that belief.

Show answer

B. The model splits its belief across the classes it knows. A Nothing or Background Noise class gives it somewhere sensible to put that belief.

Key takeaways

  • Every app runs the loop camera → model → scores → rule → action, many times a second.
  • In the exported code, the link (URL) picks the model, requestAnimationFrame keeps the loop going, and predict() returns a className and probability for every class.
  • Find classes by name, never by position, and keep the camera flip the same as in training.
  • A threshold stops unsure frames, a hold stops flickers, and a cooldown or re-arm stops repeats. Each one costs a little: missed gestures, delay, or slower repeats.

#Further reading

  • Teachable Machine image library (opens in a new tab): the official reference for tmImage.load, predict, predictTopK, and the webcam helper, including the note on flipping.
  • Speech commands README (opens in a new tab): explains every listen() option for audio models, including probabilityThreshold and overlapFactor.
  • ml5.js imageClassifier (opens in a new tab): the friendlier library used in the next lesson, with examples for Teachable Machine models.

What you'll learn

  • Load an uploaded Teachable Machine model into the p5.js Web Editor with ml5.js.
  • Show the live label and confidence on the canvas.
  • Lock in a move with a threshold and a hold time, and re-arm with the Nothing class.
  • Test the game's rules with fake data before testing with the camera, then play-test with a tally sheet.

Your rock, paper, scissors model has been a project file and a link so far. In this build it becomes a game. Hold up a sign, keep it steady while a bar fills for one second, and the computer throws its own move. Lower your hand (Nothing) to start the next round. Here's how a game moves between its two states:

The second arrow out of Result is the re-arm from the last lesson. Without it, the hand you're still holding up would play round after round by itself.

You need your model's shareable link from Module 6 and a webcam. Everything runs in the free p5.js Web Editor (opens in a new tab). This lesson page can't show the camera, so each step says what you should see.

#Step 1: Set up the sketch

  1. Open editor.p5js.org. Sign in if you want to save your work (it's free).
  2. A new sketch has three files: index.html, sketch.js, and style.css. If you don't see them, click the small arrow next to sketch.js to open the file list.
  3. Open index.html and replace everything in it with this:

The first script is p5.js, the drawing library. The second is ml5.js version 1, which knows how to load Teachable Machine models. These are the same two versions the ml5.js team uses in its own Teachable Machine example.

⚠️ Watch out

The p5.js snippet in Teachable Machine's export window was written for an older ml5.js. With today's version it stops with an error like ml5.flipImage is not a function, because ml5.js 1.0 removed that function. Use the code in this lesson, which follows the current ml5.js examples.

#Step 2: Show the camera and the model's answer

Replace everything in sketch.js with this, and paste your own link into MODEL_URL, keeping the / at the end:

Click the Play button (the triangle at the top). The browser asks for camera permission; allow it. After a few seconds you should see your mirrored webcam image with a line under it like Rock 0.98, changing as you switch signs.

What each piece does:

  • await ml5.imageClassifier(...) loads your model from the link and waits until it's ready.
  • createCapture(VIDEO, { flipped: true }) mirrors the camera, matching how Teachable Machine recorded your samples. Without it, any sign that depends on left and right is read backward.
  • classifyStart(video, gotResult) keeps classifying frames, and calls gotResult with a list of results sorted from most to least confident, so results[0] is always the top class.

If nothing appears, open the editor's Console at the bottom. A typo in the link usually shows up there as a failed download of model.json.

#Step 3: Write the "steady move" rule, and test it without a camera

The rule from the last lesson: a move counts only when the model is at least 0.9 sure and the same label has been on top for a full second. This function does that. It remembers which label it's watching (candidate) and when that label started winning (heldSince):

Predict before you read the output: when does Rock first count? The unsure Paper frame at 450 ms resets the candidate, so the second it needs starts again at 600 ms. Rock locks in at 1700 ms, the first frame that's at least 1000 ms after 600. Testing the rule on made-up frames like this is much faster than waving your hand at a camera and wondering why nothing happened.

#Step 4: Decide who wins

The game logic is a small lookup: each move beats exactly one other. Check it against all nine combinations before trusting it:

Three draws on the diagonal, and each move wins once and loses once. That's a complete, correct table.

#Step 5: Put it together

Now the game itself. draw() runs about 60 times a second; each time, it asks steadyMove whether a move has been held, and the state variable decides what that means. In ready, a held Rock, Paper, or Scissors plays a round. In result, only a held Nothing does anything: it starts the next round. The computer picks its move after yours locks in, from p5's random, so it can't cheat by watching your hand.

This is the complete sketch.js. Replace your file with it, paste your link again, and press Play:

When it runs, the top bar reads "Hold your move steady for 1 second". Raise a fist and a blue bar under the video fills over one second, then the top bar shows something like Rock vs Paper: Computer wins, and the score updates. Keep your fist up and nothing else happens. Lower your hand, wait a second, and the prompt returns.

#Step 6: Play-test with a tally sheet

A game that "seems to work" hasn't been tested. Play 10 rounds with each sign, deliberately, and write down two kinds of failure, which are Module 5's two error types wearing game clothes:

"Locked wrong move" is a false positive for the move it chose. "Never locked in" is a false negative: the model wasn't sure enough for long enough. If misses are high for one sign, try a threshold of 0.85 for that test, and see if wrong locks stay at zero. Change one setting at a time, just as you changed one thing at a time in your data.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the game need a held Nothing before the next round?

  • The move is still on top after the round ends. The re-arm makes the player do something new before another round can start.

  • It classifies whatever it sees, as often as it can.

  • The model never retrains while the game runs.

Show answer

A. The move is still on top after the round ends. The re-arm makes the player do something new before another round can start.

2You set HOLD_MS to 3000. What changes?

  • The hold time is a separate rule from the threshold.

  • A longer hold filters more flicker but adds delay, and any unsure frame restarts the wait.

  • The computer picks immediately after your move locks in.

Show answer

B. A longer hold filters more flicker but adds delay, and any unsure frame restarts the wait.

3Why test steadyMove and winner with fake data in Steps 3 and 4?

  • The sketch would run either way; the tests are for you.

  • When a rule misbehaves with the camera, you'd otherwise not know if the problem is the rule or the model.

Show answer

B. When a rule misbehaves with the camera, you'd otherwise not know if the problem is the rule or the model.

Key takeaways

  • ml5.js loads a Teachable Machine link with ml5.imageClassifier(link + "model.json"); classifyStart keeps sending results sorted by confidence.
  • Mirror the camera with { flipped: true } so the app sees what the model was trained on.
  • A state variable keeps the game's rules clear: in ready a held move plays, in result only a held Nothing re-arms.
  • Test rules on fake data first, then play-test with a tally of wrong locks (false positives) and misses (false negatives).

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a "Rock, paper, scissors, shoot!" countdown before each round and only accept a move after "shoot".
  • Make the computer smarter: have it remember your last five moves and play what beats your favorite.
  • Use Update my cloud model with your v3 model and replay your play-test. The game picks it up with no code changes, because it loads from the same link.

#Further reading

  • ml5.js imageClassifier (opens in a new tab): every option for imageClassifier and classifyStart, with live examples you can open in the p5.js Web Editor.
  • p5.js createCapture (opens in a new tab): the reference for webcam video in p5.js, including the flipped option.

m7-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find classes by name so an app survives changes to its classes.
  • Write a cooldown for an audio app and a continuous timer for a pose app.
  • Choose a threshold from logged scores by weighing missed events against false alarms.
  • Combine a threshold, hold times, and a re-arm into a small letter-typing app.

Every exercise here runs on recorded or made-up predictions, so you can test the logic right on this page. The same functions drop into the exported Teachable Machine code or a p5.js sketch, where the live model supplies the labels instead.

#Warm-up

A jump game gets these top labels, one per frame: Stand Jump Jump Stand Jump Jump Jump Stand Stand Jump. A naive game jumps every time the label changes to Jump. How many jumps? How many would you guess the player actually made?

Show solution

The label changes to Jump at frames 2, 5, and 10, so 3 jumps. The player probably made two real jumps (frames 2 to 3 and 5 to 7); the single Jump at the end could be a flicker as they settle. A hold time of two or three frames would filter it.

#Exercise 1: Fix the app that crashed after a cleanup

A wave-to-open app worked fine with the classes Nothing, Old test, Wave. Then its maker deleted the leftover Old test class, retrained, and updated the cloud model. Now it crashes:

Explain the error and rewrite the check so it can't happen again, no matter how the classes are ordered.

Need a hint?

prediction[2] meant "the third class". How many classes are there now? Look for a way to find an entry by its className.

Show solution

Wave used to be the third entry (index 2). With Old test deleted, there are only two entries, so prediction[2] is undefined, and reading .probability from undefined throws. Worse things can happen without a crash: if the classes were reordered, index 2 could silently become a different class. Look classes up by name:

The wave && part also guards against a renamed class: if no class is called Wave, the app does nothing instead of crashing.

#Exercise 2: One ring, one notification

An audio model listens with overlapFactor: 0.5, so it scores the last second of sound every half second. One doorbell ring lasts about two seconds, so it shows up in several results in a row. Write onResult(label, score, timeSec) so that a ring notifies once: notify when Doorbell scores at least 0.9, then ignore Doorbell for 10 seconds. Test it on this log:

Expected output: two notifications, at 0.5 s and 14.0 s.

Need a hint?

Keep one variable, lastNotified, starting far in the past (like -Infinity). Notify only if the score passes the threshold and at least 10 seconds have passed since lastNotified.

Show solution

The 1.0 s and 1.5 s results are the same ring, blocked by the cooldown. The 9.0 s result is blocked twice over: it's under the threshold and inside the cooldown. In the exported audio code, you'd call onResult inside recognizer.listen, using the top class from result.scores and recognizer.wordLabels().

#Exercise 3: A posture reminder that isn't a nag

A pose model reports Upright or Slouching once a second. Write onPose(label, timeSec) that reminds the user when Slouching has won for 10 seconds straight, and then doesn't remind again until the user has sat up (any Upright result) and slouched for another 10 seconds. Test it on: slouch from 0 to 14 s, upright at 15 s, slouch from 16 to 30 s.

Expected output: reminders at 10 s and 26 s only.

Need a hint?

You need two pieces of memory: when the current slouch started (slouchStart, or null while upright), and whether you've already reminded during this slouch.

Show solution

Upright is the re-arm: it clears both the timer and the reminded flag. Notice that one upright second resets everything, which suits a posture app, since sitting up briefly is exactly what you wanted.

#Exercise 4: Pick the threshold from a log

A family logged every time their doorbell detector's top class was Doorbell for a week, and marked whether the doorbell had really rung. Each dot is one event:

The family can live with a few false alarms a week but wants at most one missed ring. Count the missed rings and false alarms for thresholds 0.7, 0.8, 0.85, and 0.9, and pick one.

Need a hint?

A missed ring is a real ring below the threshold. A false alarm is "something else" at or above it.

Show solution

0.8 is the highest threshold that keeps misses at one, with three false alarms a week. At 0.9 there are no false alarms, but three visitors would be left standing outside, which is the error this family cares about most. No threshold gets both to zero, because the groups overlap; only better data (Module 5) can pull them apart.

#Exercise 5: Say "not sure" out loud

A sign-language helper shows the top label in big letters. When the model is unsure, that's misleading. Write display(top) that returns "Not sure" when the top confidence is below 0.7, and the label otherwise. Test it on the frames below.

Need a hint?

One if is enough. Decide whether exactly 0.7 counts as sure, and say which you chose.

Show solution

Here 0.7 itself counts as sure. A visible "Not sure" is honest feedback: the signer can adjust their hand instead of trusting a wrong letter, which matters most in an app meant to help someone communicate.

#Exercise 6: The letter helper

Build the logic for a fingerspelling helper with classes A, B, C, and Nothing, using this diagram:

Write update(label, confidence, nowMs) and a text variable. Rules: a letter held at 0.9 or more for 1000 ms is typed once; another letter can't be typed until Nothing has been held for 500 ms; Nothing held for 2000 ms adds one space (never two in a row, and never at the start). Test it with the stream below, which spells A, B, a pause, then A, with one flickering frame. Expected text: AB A.

Need a hint?

Reuse the candidate and since idea from the rock, paper, scissors game to measure how long the current label has been held. Then handle two cases: the label is Nothing (re-arm, maybe add a space), or it's a letter (type it if armed and held long enough).

Show solution

The unsure A at 0.55 resets the candidate, so B starts its one-second hold again at 3000 ms and is typed at 4000 ms instead of 3250 ms. That delay is the price of a rule that never types a letter it isn't sure of.

#Challenge: The real doorbell

Train an audio project with Background Noise and Doorbell (use a doorbell sound from a video if you don't have a doorbell), upload it, and connect it to your cooldown rule from Exercise 2 in the p5.js Web Editor. Use the same index.html as the rock, paper, scissors game, and start sketch.js from this pattern, which follows the ml5.js sound example:

Paste your onResult from Exercise 2 below it, and change its console.log line to set status instead. Then run a play-test like the one in the rock, paper, scissors build: ring 10 times with different background noise, and count notifications, misses, and false alarms.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what the finished capstone must include and how it will be judged.
  • Choose a project whose classes a single camera frame or one second of sound can tell apart.
  • Write a one-page plan: classes, consent, data, unseen test, costly error, app rule, and export.
  • Lay out your work as milestones, each with a clear "done when".

A recycling helper that says "blue bin" when you hold up a can. A laptop that taps you on the shoulder after ten minutes of slouching. A doorbell alert for someone wearing headphones. Each of these is a few hundred samples, one Teachable Machine model, and about a hundred lines of copied-and-edited code. You've already done every individual step. The capstone puts them together into one prototype that somebody else can try.

#The brief

Build an interactive prototype in which a Teachable Machine model (image, audio, or pose) controls something on screen. Your prototype must have:

  1. Approved data. Every person in your samples agreed to be recorded, and anyone in a shared model agreed to sharing.
  2. A trained model with a Nothing or Background Noise class, so it has an honest answer when nothing is happening.
  3. An unseen test of at least 10 items per class, recorded in different conditions from training, with a confusion matrix.
  4. One repair round: a written hypothesis about your biggest error, one targeted data change, and a retest on the same unseen items.
  5. An app that turns predictions into actions using a threshold, a hold time, and a cooldown or re-arm.
  6. A model card and a responsible export choice.
  7. A short live demo that includes at least one failure you explain.

You'll hand in your project file (.tm), your model link or downloaded files, your sketch, your project log with test sheets, and your model card. The rubric is at the end of the third capstone lesson; read it now so nothing surprises you.

#Five project ideas

Pick one, or invent your own at a similar size. The difficulty is mostly about how alike the classes are and how fussy the app's rule is.

Idea Type Classes The hard part Stretch goal
Gesture slide clicker (starter) Image Next, Back, Nothing A Nothing class that covers talking with your hands A "Pause" gesture that blanks the screen
Recycling helper screen (starter) Image Recycling, Trash, Compost, Nothing Enough different items per class; local recycling rules "Not sure, ask a person" below the threshold
Appliance or doorbell alert (intermediate) Audio Background Noise, Doorbell, Microwave beep Background noise from many rooms and times of day A visible history of alerts with times
Posture reminder (intermediate) Pose Upright, Slouching, Away Pose models care where you sit in the frame A summary of upright minutes per session
Fingerspelling practice helper (advanced) Image Four to six letters, plus Nothing Letters with similar handshapes, like A and S Spaces after a long pause, and a "Not sure" display

Two notes on the advanced idea. Leave out letters that need motion (in ASL, J and Z are drawn in the air), because a single frame can't show them. And be honest about what it is: a practice aid for a handful of letters, not a translator. Sign languages are full languages, with grammar carried by movement and facial expression. If you know someone who signs, ask them to try your helper and tell you what it gets wrong.

#Check your idea before you commit

Run three quick checks on paper. Each one has sunk real projects.

  • The one-frame test. Can a single camera frame (or one second of sound) show the difference between every pair of classes? "Waving hello" versus "waving goodbye" fails: they look the same in a frame. "Thumbs up" versus "thumbs down" passes.
  • The people test. Whose hands, faces, voices, or bodies will be in the data? If it recognizes particular people, change the idea. If other people appear, plan how you'll ask them, and what you'll do if they say no.
  • The cost test. Which mistake would hurt your user more, a false positive or a false negative? Write it down now, before you have numbers to argue with.

#The planning template

Copy this into your project log and fill in every line. If a line is hard to fill, that's useful: it's where your project is still vague.

Here's a filled-in plan for the doorbell idea, so you can see the level of detail that helps:

Notice the decisions it makes early: a third class to absorb a known false alarm, a low threshold because misses are the costly error, and a download instead of an upload because of who can be heard in the data.

#Milestones

Work in this order. Each milestone ends with something you can show, so if time runs out you still have a working, honest project.

Two pieces of advice from every past version of a project like this:

  • Record the unseen test early (M3), and never touch it. If you wait until the end, you'll be tempted to test on whatever's handy, which is usually training data.
  • Build the app (M6) with your v1 model's link if M4 runs long. Because the app loads from a link, Update my cloud model swaps in the improved model later without changing any code.

💡 Tip

Keep everything in one folder: the .tm files for each version, your test-set folder, the project log, the model card, and a copy of your sketch. When something breaks the night before the demo, you'll know exactly which version last worked.

#Before you start recording

Your plan is ready when you can answer yes to all of these:

  • Every class is defined in terms of what the camera or microphone gets, and every pair passes the one-frame test.
  • Every person who'll appear in the data has agreed, and you know whether they agreed to sharing.
  • Your unseen test plan uses conditions that are not in your data plan.
  • You've named the costly error, and your app rule leans the right way (a lower threshold if misses are worse, a higher one if false alarms are).
  • You know whether you'll upload or download, and why.

If any answer is no, fix the plan first. Changing a plan takes five minutes; re-recording a dataset takes an afternoon.

#Further reading

  • People + AI Guidebook (opens in a new tab): Google's guide to designing products that use machine learning, written for designers rather than engineers. The "User Needs + Defining Success" chapter fits this planning step.
  • Teachable Machine FAQ (opens in a new tab): links to the team's own starter projects for fruit, head tilts, and sounds, which are good models for a project of this size.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Finish each milestone with evidence in your project log before starting the next.
  • Run a repair round and show its effect with a before-and-after chart.
  • Adapt the starter sketch to your own classes, rule settings, and actions.
  • Test your app's rule on fake predictions, then with the camera or microphone.

The plan from the last lesson tells you what to build. This lesson is the how, one milestone at a time, using a recycling helper screen as the running example. Swap in your own project at every step; the moves are the same.

Milestone Done when Evidence in your log
M2 Data Every class recorded in every planned condition; v1 trained .tm file for v1, sample counts per class
M3 Test Unseen items recorded and run through v1 Test sheet with notes, confusion matrix
M4 Repair One change made, v2 retested on the same items Hypothesis, change, before-and-after numbers
M5 Export Link or files saved; model card written model-link.txt or the zip, MODEL_CARD.md
M6 App Rule passes the fake-data test and a play-test Sketch file, play-test tally

#M2: Data and model v1

Record exactly as in Module 2: short rounds, every class in every round, one condition changed per round. For the recycling helper that means a table, a plain background, and items moved through three positions and two lighting setups, with the Nothing class covering the empty table, your hands, and items being placed or removed.

Before training, check the counts. If one class is more than about 15% bigger than the others, trim it or record more of the small ones. Then train, run a quick smoke test in Preview, and save recycling-helper-v1 with the date.

Done when the log has v1's counts per class and one line about what the smoke test showed.

#M3: The unseen test

Gather items you didn't use in training, at least 10 per class, and test them in a place or light you didn't train in. For image projects, photos in a test-set folder are easiest, because you can drop the exact same files into Preview again for v2. For audio, record your test sounds with your phone's voice recorder, and play the same recordings near the microphone when you test each version. For pose, write down the exact positions and clothing so you can repeat them.

Fill in the test sheet, with a notes column, and draw the matrix with the template from Module 5's practice lesson. For the example project, the biggest cell was Compost called Trash: 4 of 10, and the notes on all four said "not fruit": coffee grounds, a paper napkin, two tea bags.

Done when the log has the sheet, the matrix, and the biggest cell circled.

#M4: One repair round

Write the hypothesis as a sentence that could turn out wrong. For the example: "Compost items that aren't fruit get called Trash because every Compost training sample was a fruit or vegetable peel."

Then make one change that tests it. Here: record 30 new Compost samples of coffee grounds, napkins, and tea bags (check that your local compost actually accepts them), and remove 30 near-duplicate peel samples to keep the classes even. Retrain, rerun the same unseen test, and compare:

This is the chart to put in your presentation. Compost jumped from 6 to 9 and nothing else moved, which is what a well-targeted change looks like. Recycling at 7 out of 10 is now the weakest class, and that's honest information for your model card, not a failure to hide. If you have time, it's your next repair round.

Done when the log has the hypothesis, the change, both sets of numbers, and a keep-or-roll-back decision.

#M5: Export and model card

Follow Module 6: run the pre-export check, choose upload or download, and write the model card with test numbers copied from your v2 sheet. Put the M4 chart's numbers in "How it was tested" and Recycling's weakness in "Known weak spots".

Done when the release folder has the link or files and a model card that passes the reader test.

#M6: The app, from a starter

This starter sketch works for any image or sound model. It uses the same index.html as the rock, paper, scissors game (p5.js and ml5.js version 1). You change only the top two sections: the settings and the actions table. The engine underneath applies a threshold, a hold time, a cooldown, and a re-arm on your idle class.

When it runs with an image model, you see the webcam with a colored message bar under it. Hold up a can, keep it still for a moment, and the bar turns blue with "Blue bin: recycling". The small line at the bottom shows what the model sees, which is invaluable while testing. Take the can away, and once Nothing has been on top for 0.8 seconds, ready flips back to true for the next item. The editor's console logs every action with a time, which is your play-test record.

#Test the engine before the camera

Here is the same decide function fed a scripted sequence: an empty table, a can held up, the can removed, a wobbly start with a banana peel, then the peel held steady. Predict how many actions fire, and when.

Two actions: Recycling about 0.8 seconds after the can appears, and Compost once the peel has been steady for 0.8 seconds and 3 seconds have passed since the last action. The can staying up for two full seconds fires only once, because the engine isn't re-armed until Nothing returns. If you change COOLDOWN_MS to 6000 and rerun it in your head, the Compost action disappears; that's the kind of setting your play-test should decide.

#Pose projects

ml5.js doesn't load Teachable Machine pose models, so pose projects start from the Javascript snippet in the export window instead. Paste the whole snippet into index.html of a new p5.js Web Editor sketch, replacing everything, and add <div id="message"></div> under the Start button. Then, just above async function init(), paste four things from the starter: the settings, your own ACTIONS table, the let candidate = ... line, and the decide function. Finally, replace the snippet's predict function with this one:

For a posture reminder, set IDLE_LABEL = "Upright", HOLD_MS = 10000, and an action such as Slouching: () => { document.getElementById("message").textContent = "Time to sit up and stretch"; }. A ten-second hold makes the reminder wait for a real slouch, and Upright re-arms it.

#When something goes wrong

Symptom Likely cause Fix
The bottom line shows the right label, but no action ever fires A name in ACTIONS doesn't match the class name exactly (recycling vs Recycling) Copy the class names from the bottom line into ACTIONS
It always says "not sure" The threshold is higher than your model's usual confidence Watch the numbers for a minute, then set THRESHOLD just below the typical score for a clear example
The first action works, then nothing ever fires again IDLE_LABEL doesn't match your idle class exactly, so the engine never re-arms Check IDLE_LABEL against the bottom line with nothing in view
Actions fire while an item is only passing through the frame The hold time is too short Raise HOLD_MS in steps of 200 and play-test again
Left and right are swapped The camera isn't mirrored like the training webcam Keep { flipped: true } (or flip = true in the pose snippet)
Nothing loads at all A typo in MODEL_URL, or the link is missing its final / Open the link in a browser tab; it should show the model's page

Done when the fake-data test behaves as you predicted, and a play-test of 10 tries per class is tallied in your log: wrong actions (false positives) and missed actions (false negatives).

💡 Tip

If your v2 model isn't ready when you start M6, build the app with the v1 link. When v2 is done, Update my cloud model and reload the sketch; the code doesn't change.

#Further reading

  • ml5.js soundClassifier (opens in a new tab): the reference for sound models in ml5.js, if your project is audio.
  • Teachable Machine pose library (opens in a new tab): the official reference for estimatePose, predict, and the drawing helpers used in the pose snippet.

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Run a final round of tests: unseen items, stress conditions, an app play-test, and a stranger test.
  • Turn stress-test results into model card entries or a final repair.
  • Polish the screen so users can see what the model sees, when it's unsure, and what happens to the camera.
  • Present the prototype in three minutes with evidence, a deliberate failure, and honest limits, and score it with the rubric.

Every year someone's prototype works perfectly at home and then, in a bright classroom with twenty people moving behind them, answers Nothing to everything. The model didn't get worse. The conditions changed, and nobody had tested those conditions. This lesson is about finding that out on a quiet afternoon instead of in front of an audience.

#Four final tests

Each test answers a different question, so you need all four.

Test Question it answers How
Unseen test How accurate is the final model on new items? Same test set as M3, final model, confusion matrix
Stress test Where does it break? 10 tries in each condition you might meet at the demo
App play-test Does the rule turn predictions into the right actions? 10 tries per class: wrong actions, missed actions, time to act
Stranger test Can someone use it without you? A classmate tries it with no help while you watch silently

The stress test is the one people skip. List the conditions your demo might bring: the room's lighting, people behind you, a different table or wall, holding items farther away, another person's hands (with their agreement), or a noisy room for audio. Then test each one, ten tries, and write down how many worked.

Two conditions fall below 7 out of 10: people moving behind, and holding items far away. For each weak condition you have three honest choices:

  1. Repair it with a targeted round, if there's time: record samples with people in the background, keeping the classes balanced.
  2. Design around it: put a line on screen ("Hold the item close to the camera") and set up your demo so the background is a wall.
  3. Document it: add it to the model card's "Known weak spots" either way.

What you can't do is leave it out. A weakness you found and explained earns more credit than one the audience finds for you.

#Polish what the user sees

A model that's 90% accurate can still feel broken if the screen gives no feedback. Go through this list with your app open:

  • Show progress while a label is held. A filling bar, like the rock, paper, scissors game's, tells the user "keep going". Without it, they move their hand just before the action fires.
  • Say "not sure" out loud. When confidence is under the threshold, show it, in words. Silence looks like a frozen app.
  • Give instructions on screen. One line, like "Hold one item close to the camera". The stranger test will show you which line is missing.
  • Never use color alone. "Blue bin: recycling" works for everyone; a blue rectangle doesn't work for someone who can't tell blue from green.
  • Say what happens to the camera. With ml5.js and Teachable Machine's code, the frames are classified inside the browser and the camera image isn't sent anywhere. Tell your users: "The camera image stays in this browser and isn't recorded."
  • Add a keyboard fallback. Some people can't make your gestures or sounds, and sometimes the demo room breaks your model. Keys that trigger the same actions fix both. Add this to the starter sketch:

keyPressed is a p5.js function that runs whenever a key goes down, and key holds which one. Because it calls the same ACTIONS table, the screen behaves identically whether the model or the keyboard triggered it.

#The rubric

Score your own project before you present. Each row is worth the points shown; "full marks" describes the top level.

Area Points Full marks Common ways to lose points
Data and consent 20 Classes defined by what the camera or mic gets; balanced counts; varied conditions; written consent covering recording and sharing Unbalanced classes; no Nothing class; people in the data who weren't asked
Testing and error analysis 20 Unseen test of 10+ per class in new conditions; confusion matrix read correctly; false positives and negatives named for the costly class Testing on training items; matrix read sideways; only overall accuracy reported
Data improvement 15 Written hypothesis, one targeted change, same-test comparison, honest keep-or-roll-back decision Several changes at once; test items moved into training; side effects ignored
App integration 20 Threshold, hold, and cooldown or re-arm, tested on fake data and play-tested; classes found by name; on-screen feedback and keyboard fallback Acting on every frame; checking classes by position; no feedback when unsure
Responsible export and model card 15 Export choice explained; labels checked; card with real test numbers, weak spots, and "don't use it for" Personal names in labels; a card with no limits; a people-recognizing model uploaded
Presentation 10 Under 3 minutes; live demo; one explained failure; before-and-after evidence Over time; hiding failures; claims with no numbers behind them

A project scoring 80 or more is complete and honest. Notice that the rubric never rewards accuracy by itself: a 75%-accurate model with a clear diagnosis, a real repair, and an honest card scores higher than a 95% model nobody tested properly.

#Where to go next

You've now done the whole loop that professional machine learning teams run: define the problem, collect data with consent, train, test on unseen data, diagnose errors, repair the data, document the model, and connect it to something people use. The tools get bigger from here, but the loop doesn't change.

  • ml5.js has ready-trained models for hands, bodies, and faces (such as handPose and bodyPose) that you can combine with your own classifiers.
  • TensorFlow.js is the library underneath everything you exported, if you want to write the model code yourself.
  • Teachable Machine's embedded image model exports to TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers, so a model can run on a small board with a camera, with no laptop at all.

Key takeaways

  • Test four ways before you present: unseen items, stress conditions, an app play-test, and a stranger using it alone.
  • For every weak condition, repair it, design around it, or document it, and always document it.
  • Polish means progress feedback, an honest "not sure", instructions, text alongside color, a camera note, and a keyboard fallback.
  • A strong demo shows a failure on purpose and backs its claims with before-and-after numbers.
